lead: The fast before Yaldo opens with two readings about light. Paul tells the Romans that the night is nearly over, so it is time to wake and dress for the day. John goes back before creation itself, to the Word who was with God and whose life is the light of all people. The child awaited at Yaldo is that Word, and love of neighbour is the clothing proper to his day.

r.h: The night is far gone
set: Chapters 12–15 of Romans draw out how those saved by grace should live. Just before this passage Paul has told the Roman Christians to pay taxes and every other debt (13:7). He now turns the word “debt” around: one debt can never be paid off, the debt of love. He then adds a reason for urgency: the time is short.
str: vv. 8–10: love is the one debt that stays open, and it fulfils the Law.
vv. 11–12a: the time: wake up, for salvation is nearer.
vv. 12b–14: the change of clothes: take off the works of darkness and put on Christ.
kw: The ordinary word for a money debt. Paul moves from the taxes of 13:7 to a debt of another kind, which grows the more it is paid.
Not clock time but the decisive moment God has given. “You know what time it is” means: you know what hour this is in God's plan.
The word for putting on clothes. Paul uses the same image for Baptism: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27).
vv: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.
Paul lists the commandments about the neighbour in v. 9 and gathers them into Leviticus 19:18. Love does not cancel the commandments; it is what they were asking for all along.
the night is far gone, the day is near. Let us then lay aside the works of darkness and put on the armor of light;
The Christian lives at the hour before dawn. It is still dark, but the darkness is no longer the truth about the world. “Armor” is a military word: this waking up involves a struggle.
Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.
Christ himself is the garment. “The flesh” in Paul is not the body as such, but human life turned in on itself.
ch: These two verses (13:13–14) are the ones St Augustine read in the garden at Milan when he heard a child's voice saying “take up and read”; he tells the story in his Confessions (Book 8), and it brought his long resistance to an end. The Catechism quotes Romans 13:8–10 on love as the fulfilment of the Law (CCC 2196), and explains the white garment of Baptism as the sign that the baptized person has “put on Christ” (CCC 1243).

r.h: The light shines in the darkness
set: These are the opening lines of the Prologue (1:1–18), the solemn poem that begins John's Gospel. Matthew and Luke begin with the birth of Jesus; John begins earlier, and his first words deliberately repeat the first words of the Bible: “In the beginning” (Genesis 1:1). A new creation is being announced, and the Creator's own Word is its source.
str: vv. 1–2: the Word and God, before all things.
v. 3: everything was made through him.
vv. 4–5: life and light, and a darkness that could not win.
kw: In the Old Testament God creates by his word (“God said”, Genesis 1) and his word is never empty (Isaiah 55:11). Greek thinkers also used logos for the reason ordering the world. John says that this Word is a person.
John uses the verb of continuing existence for the Word (“was”), and a different verb for created things (“came into being”, v. 3). The Word did not begin; everything else did.
The Greek can mean “seize, overcome” and also “grasp, understand”. The NRSV and the POC take the first sense; both senses are true of the darkness.
vv: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

In three short steps: the Word existed, he is distinct from God the Father (“with God”), and he is himself God. The Council of Nicaea (325) defended exactly this against Arius, who taught that the Son was a creature.
All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.

A note on the text. The oldest manuscripts have no punctuation, and the end of v. 3 can be read two ways. The NRSV joins “What has come into being” to v. 4, as many early Christian writers did; the POC ends the sentence at v. 3, as others did. The faith is the same in both.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.
“Shines” is in the present tense, “did not overcome” in the past. The struggle has been decided, and the light goes on shining.
ch: The Catechism takes this passage as the New Testament's revelation that God created everything by the eternal Word (CCC 291), and says that the Apostles confessed Jesus to be the Word who was with God and is God (CCC 241). The Creed the Church prays at every Holy Qurbono echoes v. 3: “through him all things were made”.

qa: If the Word “was God”, are there two Gods?

No. John says both that the Word was “with God” and that he “was God”. The Church expresses this by confessing one God in three persons: the Son is truly God and truly distinct from the Father (CCC 253–254).
rite: For the Malankara faithful the Twenty-Five Days' Fast before Yaldo begins today, with prayer, fasting and almsgiving (1–24 December). Today's readings give it a clear aim. To fast is to take off the works of darkness, and to give alms is to pay something on the debt of love, so that the Word who shines in the darkness may find a home.
study: Paul calls love a debt that stays open. Whom do I owe love to, and have been putting off paying, in this fast?
“The light shines in the darkness.” Where in my family or parish do I need to believe this today?

lead: Today's readings are about the mouth. Paul asks how anyone can believe without a preacher, and calls beautiful the feet of those who bring the good news. Jesus asks that the same mouth be simply truthful, with no need of oaths. The one who carries the word of God must be someone whose own word can be trusted.

r.h: How beautiful are the feet
set: In chapters 9–11 Paul wrestles with the question of why most of his own people have not yet come to believe in Jesus. He has just quoted the prophet Joel: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved” (10:13). That promise raises the question these verses answer: how does anyone come to call on him?
str: vv. 14–15a: a chain of four questions, worked backward: call, believe, hear, proclaim, be sent.
v. 15b: the answer from Scripture, Isaiah 52:7.
kw: From the same verb as “apostle”, one who is sent. Preaching is not a personal career; it begins with a sending.
The verb behind “gospel”. In Isaiah 52:7 the messenger runs to tell ruined Zion that God reigns and the exile is ending.
The word is related to hōra, “hour, season”, so it can also suggest “coming at the right time”. The tired feet of a messenger are beautiful because of the news they bring.
vv: And how are they to hear without someone to proclaim him?
Faith reaches people through people. God could act otherwise, but this is the way he has chosen: a human voice.
And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”
Nobody looks at the feet of a traveller and calls them beautiful: they are dusty and cracked. Isaiah sees them that way because of the good news they carry.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it teaches about the sacred ministry: no one can give himself the mandate and mission to proclaim the Gospel; it must be received from Christ through the Church (CCC 875). At the same time every baptized person shares in this mission by word and life (CCC 900).

r.h: Let your word be Yes or No
set: This is the fourth of the six sayings in the Sermon on the Mount that begin “You have heard… But I say to you” (5:21–48). The Law forbade false oaths and required vows to be kept (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21). People used oaths to make their word stronger, and could also swear by something other than God's name in the hope of avoiding God's judgment. Jesus goes to the root.
str: v. 33: the old teaching.
vv. 34–36: do not swear: heaven, earth, Jerusalem and your own head all belong to God.
v. 37: a plain Yes or No.
kw: To call on God or on something sacred as a guarantee that what you say is true.
A simple word, meaning what it says. No additional guarantee is needed.
The Greek can be read as “the evil one” (NRSV, POC) or “evil”. The need for oaths comes from a world where lies are expected.
vv: But I say to you, Do not swear at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God,
Heaven as God's throne and earth as his footstool come from Isaiah 66:1. You cannot swear by anything and leave God out of it, because all of it is his.
And do not swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.
Even your own head is not under your control. We cannot guarantee our promises from our own resources. Hence the humility of a plain word.
Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’; anything more than this comes from the evil one.
If I need a special oath to be believed, my ordinary speech has lost its value. Jesus wants the whole of life to be truthful, not only the solemn moments. Compare James 5:12.
ch: The Catechism sets this teaching under the second commandment (CCC 2153). It adds that, following St Paul, who himself calls God to witness (2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20), the tradition of the Church has understood Jesus' words as not excluding oaths made for grave and right reasons, for example in court (CCC 2154).

qa: So is it wrong to take an oath in court, or vows at ordination or in religious life?

No. The Church has understood Jesus to forbid the casual and false use of oaths, and the need for them that comes from a lying heart. An oath for a grave and right reason remains lawful (CCC 2154). The aim of Jesus' teaching is that every word we say should be as true as if it were sworn.
study: Who brought the good news to me? Whose “beautiful feet” do I remember with gratitude, and whose door could I walk to?
Are there situations in which people cannot rely on my Yes or my No? What would need to change?

lead: On the day the Church remembers St Francis Xavier, the readings show what a missionary is. Paul changes himself, not the Gospel, so that all kinds of people can receive it. The risen Lord sends disciples whose faith he has just had to rebuke, to tell the news to the whole creation. The mission rests on Christ's sending and not on the strength of those he sends.

r.h: All things to all people
set: Chapters 8–10 deal with a practical quarrel in Corinth: may Christians eat meat offered to idols? Paul says that knowledge is not enough; love for the weaker brother or sister must decide. In chapter 9 he gives himself as an example of someone who gives up his rights: as an apostle he could expect to be supported, yet he earns his own living. These verses state the principle behind it.
str: v. 19: the paradox: free, yet a slave of all.
vv. 20–22a: the groups he serves: Jews, those under the Law, those outside the Law, the weak.
vv. 22b–23: the aim: to save some, for the sake of the Gospel.
kw: I have made myself a slave
A strong word. In a society with many slaves, a free man choosing this for himself was startling. Compare Christ, who took “the form of a slave” (Philippians 2:7).
A word from business, used five times in these verses. Paul's only profit is people won for Christ.
Paul does not stand outside the Gospel as its salesman. He hopes to share in its blessings himself, alongside those he serves.
vv: To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews.
Paul is himself a Jew and proud of it (Romans 11:1). He means that he kept Jewish customs among Jews where doing so was no obstacle to the Gospel (compare Acts 16:3; 21:26).
I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some.

This is not saying whatever pleases people. In v. 21 Paul insists he is “under Christ’s law”, and in this same letter he rebukes the Corinthians firmly. What changes is the messenger: his habits, his comfort, his rights. The message does not change.
I do it all for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings.
ch: The Church speaks of this today as inculturation: the Gospel enters a people's culture, purifying and raising what is good in it (CCC 854; St John Paul II, Redemptoris Missio 52). St Francis Xavier lived the passage in his own way. Sailing east for the first time at 35, he had the basic prayers and commandments put into the language of the fishing people of South India, and later went on to the Malay world and Japan.

r.h: Go into all the world
set: A note on the text. These verses belong to the “longer ending” of Mark (16:9–20), which is missing from two of the oldest Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) and differs in style from the rest of the Gospel. Many scholars therefore think it was added early by another hand. It was known by the second century and the Church receives it as inspired Scripture, part of the canon. It gathers up what the other Gospels and Acts report of the risen Lord.
str: v. 14: the rebuke of the Eleven at table.
vv. 15–16: the sending, and what depends on the response.
vv. 17–18: the signs that will accompany believers.
kw: Literally “unbelief” and “hardness of heart”. Jesus has used the second word of others (Mark 10:5). Now it describes his own closest friends, and he sends them anyway.
“The whole creation”: no nation, people or corner of the world lies outside the good news.
Not displays of power for their own sake, but pointers that confirm the word (16:20).
vv: And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
This comes straight after the rebuke. The Church's mission has never depended on the disciples being impressive.
The one who believes and is baptized will be saved; but the one who does not believe will be condemned.
Faith and Baptism go together, and the Gospel calls for a decision. On those who through no fault of their own do not know Christ, see the question below.
they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.”

Acts reports several of these signs: tongues (Acts 2:4), demons cast out (16:18), the snake at Malta (28:3–6) and hands laid on the sick (28:8). Nothing here tells Christians to test God by handling snakes on purpose; Jesus himself refused to put God to the test (Matthew 4:7).
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 16 in teaching that the Lord tied the forgiveness of sins to faith and Baptism (CCC 977), and v. 18 in teaching about the sacrament for the sick (CCC 1507). St Francis Xavier, whom Pope Pius XI named a patron of the missions in 1927 together with St Thérèse of Lisieux, took “all the world” literally: he died in 1552 on the island of Shangchuan, within sight of the China he longed to enter.

qa: Does this mean that everyone who has not believed is condemned?

No one is condemned for what he could not know. Vatican II teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, yet seek God sincerely and try to follow their conscience, moved by grace, may attain eternal salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). This never lessens the Church's duty to proclaim Christ (CCC 848).
rite: St Francis Xavier belonged to the Latin Church, but his story touches Kerala and South India closely. He worked on the Fishery Coast and in Travancore and, according to his own letters, visited the tomb of St Thomas at Mylapore in 1545. The faith of the St Thomas Christians was far older than his coming. Today Malankara Catholics may honour him as a brother in the same mission, and ask what it means in our own time to go to those who have not yet heard.
study: Paul gave up his rights so that others could hear the Gospel. Which of my comforts or habits stand in the way of someone meeting Christ?
Jesus rebukes the Eleven and sends them in the same scene. What does that say to me when I feel unworthy to speak of my faith?

lead: Paul says that faith comes by hearing, and asks whether the word has really reached the whole world. Jesus says that the word heard has to reach the heart, down to the anger we keep inside and the brother we have not forgiven. Today's saint, St John of Damascus, adds that since the Word became flesh, the eye too may receive him in holy icons.

r.h: Faith comes from what is heard
set: Paul is still answering the question of Romans 9–11: why have so many in Israel not yet accepted Jesus as Messiah? He rules out the idea that they had no chance to hear. He writes with sorrow and love for his own people (9:1–3), and he goes on to declare that God has not rejected them (11:1). Chapters 9–11 must be read together; a verse taken alone can easily mislead.
str: v. 17: the principle: faith comes from hearing, and hearing from the word of Christ.
v. 18: have they not heard? Psalm 19:4.
vv. 19–20: did Israel not understand? Deuteronomy 32:21 and Isaiah 65:1.
kw: The word means both the act of hearing and the message heard. Christian faith is not an idea we think up; it comes to us from outside.
This can mean the word that comes from Christ or the word about Christ (as the POC takes it). Some later manuscripts read “the word of God”.
From Deuteronomy 32:21. In 11:11–14 Paul explains the aim: the faith of the nations is meant to stir Israel to come closer, not to replace it.
vv: So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
The preaching of the Church is more than information. Christ himself speaks through it.
for “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

Psalm 19 speaks of the heavens telling God's glory without words. Paul applies the verse to the preachers of the Gospel. He means the word has gone out far and wide, not that every individual has already heard.
“I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.”
God takes the first step. The nations who were not looking for him are Paul's example, and all of us who did nothing to earn the Gospel stand among them.
ch: St Paul VI quotes v. 17 to show that preaching by word remains necessary in every age (Evangelii Nuntiandi 42). St John of Damascus, whom the Church remembers today, shows how the same Gospel can also reach us through the eye. The Catechism quotes his teaching that the God who had no body has now become visible in the flesh, so that we may make an image of what we have seen of God (CCC 1159), and adds that image and word illuminate each other (CCC 1160).

r.h: First be reconciled
set: This is the first of the six sayings in Matthew 5 that begin “You have heard”. Jesus has just said that he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (5:17). So he does not weaken “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13); he takes it down to its root in the heart. The word “council” in v. 22 refers to the Sanhedrin, the high court.
str: vv. 21–22: from murder to anger and insult, with rising penalties.
vv. 23–24: at the altar: go first and be reconciled.
vv. 25–26: on the road to court: settle while there is time.
kw: From the Hebrew gê hinnōm, the valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). It became an image for final ruin.

An insult that denies a person's worth. The word before it in the Greek is the Aramaic raka, “empty-head”, which the NRSV renders “if you insult”. Contempt treats a person as nothing, and it is murder begun in the mind.
A very small Roman coin (quadrans). “The last penny” means the debt will be paid in full.
vv: So when you are offering your gift at the altar, if you remember that your brother or sister has something against you,
Note who has the grievance. It is not “if you are angry with someone”, but if someone has something against you. Then you take the first step.
leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.
In the Temple this was a startling picture. Worship stops for the sake of reconciliation. Worship itself is not cancelled: “then come and offer”.
Truly I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
A warning given while there is still time. The picture is of debts left unsettled until it is too late.
ch: The Catechism says that in recalling this commandment the Lord adds the prohibition of anger, hatred and vengeance (CCC 2262, 2302), and that from the Sermon on the Mount onward he insists on reconciliation with one's brother before presenting an offering at the altar (CCC 2608). The Didache, a very early Christian manual, already applies these words to the Eucharist: no one at odds with a companion should join the gathering until reconciled, so that the sacrifice may not be defiled (in substance, Didache 14).

qa: Is all anger a sin?

No. Jesus himself looked at people “with anger” at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5), and Paul writes, “Be angry but do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). The passion of anger is not sinful in itself. It becomes sin when we consent to the wish to harm, when we feed it and hold on to it (CCC 1767; 2302).
rite: Before the great thanksgiving of the anaphora, the Holy Qurbono has the sign of peace passed from the altar to the people. Matthew 5:23–24 is the Gospel behind that moment. In this fast, today's reading asks each of us to ask: who has something against me, and what will I do about it before Yaldo? St John of Damascus, a monk of the Lavra of St Sabbas near Jerusalem, is honoured in East and West; he gives a reason for the icons before which Eastern Christians pray.
study: Faith comes from what is heard. How much time do I give to hearing the word of Christ during this fast?
Is there anyone who has something against me? What first step can I take before I next go to the Holy Qurbono?

lead: Paul tells Timothy to train himself in godliness as an athlete trains his body, which is a fitting word in a fast. John shows the crowd, the temple police and the authorities divided over Jesus, and one man, Nicodemus, asking only that he be given a fair hearing. Training in godliness begins with this kind of honest listening.

r.h: Train yourself in godliness
set: The First Letter to Timothy, received by the Church among the letters of St Paul, gives guidance to a young church leader at Ephesus. Just before this passage it warns of teachers who “forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods”, and answers that “everything created by God is good” (4:3–4). So the training Paul now commends is not contempt for the body or for food. Christian fasting does not come from thinking creation is bad.
str: v. 6: the good servant, nourished on sound teaching.
vv. 7–8: leave aside the myths; train in godliness, which is useful for this life and the next.
vv. 9–10: a trustworthy saying, and the reason for the effort: hope in the living God.
kw: From the word for athletic training, which also gives us “gymnasium”. Godliness does not happen by itself; it needs regular practice, as a body does.
A favourite word of these letters: reverence for God lived out in daily conduct. The POC has “ദൈവഭക്തി” in v. 7 and “ആത്മീയത” in v. 8.
A formula found five times in the letters to Timothy and Titus (for example 1 Timothy 1:15), which marks a saying the Church can rely on.
vv: Have nothing to do with profane myths and old wives’ tales. Train yourself in godliness,
The contrast is between speculation that goes nowhere and practice that changes a life.
for, while physical training is of some value, godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for both the present life and the life to come.
Bodily training is not despised: it has “some value”. But its benefits end with this life, while godliness carries over.
For to this end we toil and struggle, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
“Struggle” translates a word used for athletic contests. The effort is not self-improvement: it is hope in a God who wants to save all (compare 1 Timothy 2:4).
ch: “There is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle,” says the Catechism, and spiritual progress requires ascesis and mortification (CCC 2015). The two saints of today lived this in different ways. Mar Saba spent long years in the desert and founded a community of monks there. St Clement of Alexandria wrote a work called The Tutor (Paedagogus), in which Christ is the one who patiently trains Christians in daily conduct.

r.h: Never has anyone spoken like this
set: The scene is the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem (7:2). On its last day Jesus has cried out, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me” (7:37). The crowd is now divided. Some think he is “the prophet” like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15; some, the Messiah; some object that he is from Galilee. Temple police sent earlier to arrest him (7:32) come back without him.

John does not speak here of a whole people rejecting Jesus. He shows a division among ordinary people and among the authorities themselves, and a member of the council who speaks up for him. The Church firmly teaches that the Jewish people as a whole must not be blamed for what happened to Jesus (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
str: vv. 40–44: the crowd divided: prophet, Messiah, or neither?
vv. 45–49: the police return: “Never has anyone spoken like this!” The Pharisees' scorn.
vv. 50–52: Nicodemus asks for a hearing and is mocked.
v. 53: all go home.
kw: The word from which “schism” comes. It occurs three times in John, always of people divided over Jesus (7:43; 9:16; 10:19). His word forces a decision.
Attendants who kept order in the Temple under the authorities. They came to arrest him, and his words stopped them.
A harsh word from a few leaders, in scorn of ordinary people who have not studied. John quotes it to show how pride in learning can blind.
vv: Has not the scripture said that the Messiah is descended from David and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?”

The speakers are right about the Scriptures (2 Samuel 7:12; Micah 5:2). John leaves an irony for his Christian readers, who know the stories of Jesus' birth: the objection is mistaken because the speakers do not know who stands before them.
The police answered, “Never has anyone spoken like this!”
Men sent with authority return disarmed by a voice. They offer no argument; they only report what they heard.
“Our law does not judge people without first giving them a hearing to find out what they are doing, does it?”
Nicodemus, who came “by night” (3:2), speaks by day now. Deuteronomy 1:16–17 commands fair hearings. He will appear once more, bringing myrrh and aloes for the burial (19:39).
[[ Then each of them went home,

A note on the text. The NRSV brackets v. 53 because it begins the story of the woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11), which is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts of John. The Church receives that passage as inspired Scripture all the same.
ch: The Catechism points to this scene to show that the religious authorities in Jerusalem were not of one mind about Jesus: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were secret disciples, and there was long-standing dissension about him (CCC 595). The objection about Galilee reminds Christians that human knowledge, even of Scripture, needs humility before the living Word.

qa: Did no prophet come from Galilee?

The Pharisees' claim in v. 52 is spoken in anger and is not strictly accurate: 2 Kings 14:25 says the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher, a town in the region later called Galilee. John simply reports the words, and his readers can see how little the argument holds.
rite: Mar Saba (died 532) founded the Great Lavra in the Judean desert, which still has monks today; St John of Damascus, remembered yesterday, lived there. St Clement of Alexandria (died around 215) was an early Christian teacher who took the wisdom of the Greeks seriously and led it to Christ. Between them they show the two sides of the Eastern Christian inheritance: the desert and the school. A fast in the Malankara tradition needs both: self-denial and the hearing of the word.
study: What does regular “training in godliness” look like for me in this fast? Name one daily practice.
Like Nicodemus, have I ever had to ask for a fair hearing for someone others were dismissing? Have I been the one dismissing?

lead: On the fourth Sunday of Suboro the Church gathers around a cradle in the hill country of Judea. The Evening Gospel already gives the song that follows today's story: Zechariah's Benedictus, which greets “the dawn from on high” (Luke 1:67–80). The Old Testament lessons set John among other children given by God: Moses, whom Pharaoh's daughter named because “I drew him out of the water” (Exodus 2:1–10); Samuel, asked of the Lord and given back to him (1 Samuel 1:19–28); the psalm's word, “Sons are indeed a heritage from the Lord” (Psalm 127:3); and Isaiah's promise to Zion that “you shall be called by a new name” (Isaiah 62:2). The Catholic Epistle warns us to “test the spirits” (1 John 4:1), which is John's own work of telling truth from error.

The three readings studied here share one pattern. A woman who could not have children bears a child by God's gift, and that child is given back for God's purposes: Hannah and Samuel, Sarah and Isaac in Paul's argument, Elizabeth and John. The names carry the message. Hannah means “grace”; John, from the same Hebrew root, means “the Lord has been gracious”; Zechariah means “the Lord has remembered”. Remembering, grace and giving back are the key words of this Sunday.

r.h: For this child I prayed
set: The story comes at the end of the time of the Judges, when Israel had no king and the sanctuary stood at Shiloh. Elkanah has two wives. Peninnah has children; Hannah has none, and Peninnah taunts her year after year (1:2–7). At Shiloh Hannah weeps and makes a vow: if God gives her a son, she will give him back to God all his life, and no razor will touch his head (1:11). The old priest Eli at first thinks she is drunk, and then blesses her (1:12–18). Today's reading tells how the prayer was answered and the vow kept.
The child will become the prophet who anoints Israel's first kings. A nation's future begins with one woman's prayer that no one else understood.
str: vv. 19–20: the Lord remembers Hannah; Samuel is born and named.
vv. 21–23: Elkanah goes up to Shiloh; Hannah stays until the child is weaned.
vv. 24–25: she brings the child to the house of the Lord, with her offering.
vv. 26–28: her words to Eli: the prayer heard and the child given.

¶ A note on the text. At two points the NRSV follows ancient witnesses other than the traditional Hebrew text: the last words of v. 22 (“I will offer him as a nazirite for all time”) come from a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel, and “a three-year-old bull” in v. 24 agrees with that scroll and the Greek, where the traditional Hebrew has “three bulls”. The POC agrees on the bull, and does not have the words about the nazirite in v. 22.
kw: In the Bible God's remembering is not a recovery from forgetfulness. It means that he acts on what he has promised or been asked. Hannah used the same word in her vow: “remember me” (1:11). The name Zechariah comes from this verb.

The word Hannah keeps returning to. “I have asked him” (v. 20), “the petition” (v. 27), “I have lent him”, literally “I have let him be asked for” (v. 28). What was asked from God is now handed over to God.
One set apart for God, marked by uncut hair and no wine (Numbers 6). The angel will say something similar of John: “He must never drink wine or strong drink” (Luke 1:15).
From the root ḥ-n-n, to be gracious. The name John (Hebrew yôḥānān) comes from the same root.
vv: Elkanah knew his wife Hannah, and the Lord remembered her.
Two actions in one sentence, the human one and the divine one. A child is the fruit of both.
She named him Samuel, for she said, “I have asked him of the Lord.”

The explanation is a play on sound and not a dictionary meaning: the verb “ask” sounds closer to the name Saul. Scholars usually take Samuel to mean something like “name of God”. Hannah's point is clear: this name will remind her where he came from. Here it is the mother who names him, just as Elizabeth is the first to speak the name of John.
For this child I prayed; and the Lord has granted me the petition that I made to him.
A moment of quiet joy. She stands at the very spot where she wept (v. 26) and points to the child.
Therefore I have lent him to the Lord; as long as he lives, he is given to the Lord.”

“Lent” is the NRSV's way of keeping the wordplay on “ask”, but this loan is not returned: it lasts “as long as he lives”. The POC says plainly “I have consecrated him”. What she prayed for most, she gives away.
ch: The Catechism names Hannah among the holy women of the Old Covenant through whom God, against all human expectation, shows his faithfulness to his promises, and who prepare for Mary (CCC 489). It teaches that a child is not something owed to anyone but a gift (CCC 2378), and that parents must respect and encourage the vocation of their children (CCC 2232). St John Chrysostom preached a series of sermons on Hannah, holding her up as a model of persevering prayer and of parents who give their children to God (in substance).

r.h: Children of the promise
set: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey, which he had founded among Gentiles. Other Christian teachers have come after him, telling them they must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to belong fully to God's people. Paul's whole letter says no: we are saved by faith in Christ, and the Gentiles need not become Jews first. This passage is the last of his arguments from Scripture.

The story he uses is in Genesis 16 and 21. God promised Abraham a son by his wife Sarah, who was barren. Impatient, they tried another way, through the slave woman Hagar, who bore Ishmael. Later Isaac was born to Sarah, as God had said.

This is an argument among Christians about the Gentile converts. It is not a judgment on the Jewish people or on Judaism. The same Paul writes elsewhere of his people that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).
str: v. 21: the challenge: you want the Law? Then listen to it.
vv. 22–23: two sons, two mothers: by the flesh, and by the promise.
vv. 24–27: two covenants: Hagar, Sinai and the present Jerusalem; the free woman, the Jerusalem above, “our mother”, with Isaiah 54:1.
vv. 28–31: the application: you are children of the promise, like Isaac.
kw: Literally “these things are spoken in another sense”. Paul does not deny that the events happened. He reads them as pointing beyond themselves to Christ and the Church. Christian interpreters usually call this typology.
Isaac was born not by human planning but because God said so. The same is true of every believer, who is a child of God by grace and not by descent or achievement.
The city of God, already present and yet still to come. Compare Hebrews 12:22 and Revelation 21:2. Paul calls her “our mother”, and Christians from every nation belong to her.
Paul's contrast. The freedom in question is the one he speaks of in the next verse (5:1): “For freedom Christ has set us free.”
vv: Now this is an allegory: these women are two covenants.
Paul compares two ways of relating to God: trying to secure our place by our own observance, and receiving it as a gift.
But the other woman corresponds to the Jerusalem above; she is free, and she is our mother.
The Church's title of “mother” goes back to this verse.
For it is written, “Rejoice, you childless one, you who bear no children,

This is Isaiah 54:1, spoken to Jerusalem in exile, who seemed like a barren wife. Paul reads it of the Church from the nations. Every barren mother in today's readings stands behind this verse: Sarah, Hannah, Elizabeth.
Now you, my friends, are children of the promise, like Isaac.
Here is the link with the Gospel. John is a child of promise by the angel's word (Luke 1:13). Through Baptism, so are we.
“Drive out the slave and her child;

Sarah's words (Genesis 21:10), applied by Paul to the teaching that was enslaving the Galatians, not to any people. Genesis itself shows God hearing Hagar and her boy in the desert and caring for them (21:17–20).
ch: The Second Vatican Council, followed by the Catechism, gathers this verse among the images of the Church: she is “that Jerusalem which is above” and “our mother” (Lumen Gentium 6; CCC 757). On reading the Old Testament in the light of Christ, the Catechism explains typology: the types do not cancel the value of the Old Testament, which keeps its own worth as revelation (CCC 128–130). St John Chrysostom, a son of Antioch, comments that Paul here uses the word “allegory” loosely, for what is properly a type: the events really happened, and they also point beyond themselves (in substance). This care for the history is a mark of the Antiochene way of reading Scripture, to which the Malankara Church is heir.

r.h: His name is John
set: Luke's first chapter sets two births side by side: an angel announces John to Zechariah in the Temple (1:5–25), and Jesus to Mary at Nazareth (1:26–38). The two mothers meet (1:39–56). Now John is born, and soon Jesus will be (2:1–20). John's story is told so that we will see he prepares for Jesus and is less than him.

Zechariah and Elizabeth were both “getting on in years”, and she was barren (1:7). When the angel promised a son, Zechariah asked for proof. He was told he would be unable to speak “because you did not believe my words” (1:20). He has now been silent for the whole of the pregnancy.

Background. The Law commanded circumcision on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). Luke shows the child being named at the same time, as he does again with Jesus (2:21). A family name would normally be expected.
str: vv. 57–58: the birth, and the neighbours' joy.
vv. 59–61: the eighth day and the argument about the name.
vv. 62–63: the father is asked; he writes on a tablet.
v. 64: his mouth is opened, and he praises God.
vv. 65–66: fear, talk across the hill country, and the question: what will this child be?
kw: Literally “made his mercy great”. It is the same verb as Mary's “My soul magnifies the Lord” (1:46). God magnifies his mercy, and the human response is to magnify him.
This fulfils the angel's word: “many will rejoice at his birth” (1:14). A gift to one family becomes joy for a whole village.
Hebrew yôḥānān, “the Lord has been gracious”. The name comes not from the family tree but from God (1:13). It tells the story of this child and of the time he introduces.
An Old Testament phrase for God's active power with a person, used for example of Elijah (1 Kings 18:46). Luke uses it to close the scene and to open John's future.
vv: Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown his great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
For people of that time, a barren woman bore a shame she herself had named (1:25). The whole community now sees the shame removed.
But his mother said, “No; he is to be called John.”
Elizabeth stands firm alone against the custom and the crowd. On how she knew the name, see the question below.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And all of them were amazed.

The relatives make signs to him (v. 62), so he was perhaps deaf as well as mute; the Greek word in 1:22 can mean both. He does not write “let his name be”. He writes “is”. The name has already been given by God, and Zechariah only confirms it.
Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue freed, and he began to speak, praising God.

Having obeyed in the matter where he had doubted, he speaks. His first use of a restored voice is blessing. The Greek here is “blessing God”, and it leads directly to the Benedictus: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (1:68).
All who heard them pondered them and said, “What then will this child become?” For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him.
This is a question every parent might ask at a cradle. Luke answers it in Zechariah's song: “you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High” (1:76).
ch: The Catechism calls John “the Lord's immediate precursor or forerunner” (CCC 523). He is filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb, and in him the Spirit concludes the speaking through the prophets (CCC 717–720). St Augustine draws out the meaning in a sermon for John's feast: John is the voice and Christ is the Word; the voice passes, and the Word remains (in substance, Sermon 293). The Catechism also connects names with vocation: God calls each one by name, and the Christian receives a name in the Church at Baptism (CCC 2156–2158).

qa: How did Elizabeth know the name John, if Zechariah could not speak?

Luke does not say. Zechariah may have written it for her during those months, since he could write (1:63). Some commentators have also seen a prompting of the Holy Spirit, who had already filled her (1:41). Luke's interest lies elsewhere: husband and wife, separately, agree with what God has said, against everyone's expectations.
Did Hannah abandon her child?

No. A child in that culture could be nursed for up to three years (compare 2 Maccabees 7:27), so Samuel was small but no longer an infant. She saw him every year and “used to make for him a little robe” (1 Samuel 2:19). She handed him over to God's service, as parents still do in a different way when a son or daughter enters the priesthood or religious life. God then gave her more children (2:21).
Does Galatians 4 mean God has rejected the Jewish people?

No. Paul is opposing Christian teachers who wanted to impose circumcision on Gentile believers. He writes of Israel, “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). The Church teaches that the Jews must not be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4), and she recognizes their special relation to God (CCC 839).
rite: Malankara readers hear the story of this Sunday in stages. The Syriac liturgical day begins in the evening, so the Evening Gospel gives Zechariah's song before the morning Gospel tells of the birth that caused it. Suboro, the season of “good news”, is a season of annunciations and births: the Sunday after this one is that of the angel's appearance to St Joseph, then comes the Sunday before Yaldo, and then Yaldo itself. John will return at Denho, standing at the Jordan. In the middle of the Twenty-Five Days' Fast, this Sunday invites families to thank God for each child by name, to pray for those who long for a child and do not have one, and to ask of every little one in the parish: what then will this child become?
study: Hannah gave back what she prayed for most. What gift of God am I holding too tightly?
“Children of the promise”: how does knowing that I am God's child by grace, not by my achievements, change the way I pray?
Zechariah's silence ended in praise. What has God taught me in a time when I could not speak or did not understand?
What do I want the children of my family and parish to become? What am I doing to help them hear God's call?

lead: On the memorial of St Ambrose, Paul writes from prison to tell Timothy not to be ashamed and to guard what has been entrusted to him. Jesus, on the night before his death, tells disciples who are about to run away that he has conquered the world. Courage in both readings comes from knowing whom we have trusted, not from any strength of our own.

r.h: Guard the good treasure
set: This letter presents Paul in chains and near the end of his life: “the time of my departure has come” (4:6). Timothy seems young and easily discouraged, which is why Paul has just reminded him that “God did not give us a spirit of cowardice” (1:7). What will happen to the Gospel when the apostle is gone? The passage answers: it is God's work, and it has been entrusted to faithful hands.
str: v. 8: do not be ashamed; share in suffering.
vv. 9–10: the reason: a short summary of the Gospel, from before the ages to the appearing of Christ.
vv. 11–12: Paul's own example: “I am not ashamed”.
vv. 13–14: hold the pattern, guard the treasure.
kw: what is entrusted, the good treasure (vv. 12, 14)
A legal word for something left in another's safekeeping, to be returned intact. It appears in vv. 12 and 14 and in 1 Timothy 6:20. The Church's phrase “the deposit of faith” comes from here.
A word used for a god or a ruler showing himself. Here it means Christ's coming in the flesh. The letters to Timothy also use it for his return (2 Timothy 4:1).
An outline or model for copying. Timothy does not make up the teaching; he holds to the pattern he received.
vv: who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace.
This grace was given “before the ages began”. Before Timothy was afraid, and before the first prison, God had already acted.
who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.
“Abolished”: made powerless. Death still comes, but it no longer has the last word. A prisoner writing with death ahead of him is the one who says so.
But I am not ashamed, for I know the one in whom I have put my trust, and I am sure that he is able to guard until that day what I have entrusted to him.

Not “I know what” but “I know the one”: faith is first of all trust in a person. The Greek says “my deposit”, which can mean what Paul has entrusted to God (NRSV) or what God has entrusted to Paul (the way the POC takes it).
Guard the good treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit living in us.
Keeping the faith is not only a human effort. The Spirit is the true guardian, and Timothy works with him.
ch: The Catechism says that the apostles entrusted the “sacred deposit” of the faith, contained in Scripture and Tradition, to the whole Church, and cites this passage (CCC 84). St Ambrose, Bishop of Milan from 374, is an example of such guarding. He held firm against the Arian party, even when pressed by the imperial court, and at Easter in 387 he baptized Augustine, who would hand the faith on to many generations.

r.h: Take courage; I have conquered the world
set: These are the last words of the Farewell Discourse (John 13–16), spoken at the table on the night before the Passion. After this comes only the prayer of Jesus to the Father (John 17), and then the arrest. The disciples think that at last they understand. Jesus knows that within hours they will scatter.
str: vv. 25–28: from figures to plain speech: the Father himself loves you. Jesus came from the Father and returns to him.
vv. 29–30: the disciples' confident response.
vv. 31–32: “Do you now believe?” They will scatter, but he is not alone.
v. 33: peace, trouble and victory.
kw: Open, unhindered speech. It is also the confidence of those who may speak openly to God (Hebrews 4:16).
Literally “pressure, crushing”: the NRSV has “persecution”, the POC ഞെരുക്കം. Jesus promises it. He does not promise his followers an easy road.
A Greek perfect tense: a victory already won, whose effects last. He says it before the Cross. See 1 John 5:4: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith”.
vv: for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.
This is the “plain speech” about the Father. Jesus does not stand between us and an unwilling God. The Father himself loves.
The hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each one to his home, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone because the Father is with me.

He says this without any bitterness, naming the coming failure so that it will not destroy them afterward. The cry of Psalm 22 from the Cross (Mark 15:34) must be read together with this confidence: that psalm itself ends in trust.
I have said this to you, so that in me you may have peace. In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!”
“In me” and “in the world” are the two places where a disciple lives at once. Peace does not mean that the trouble is gone; it means that the trouble has been defeated.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 33 when it teaches about the virtue of fortitude, which enables us to conquer fear, even fear of death (CCC 1808). On prayer “in my name” (v. 26), it teaches that faith in the Son brings the disciples into the knowledge of the Father (CCC 2614). When St Ambrose faced pressure in Milan, he and his people kept watch in the church; St Augustine records that it was then that hymns and psalms began to be sung there after the manner of the Eastern regions (in substance, Confessions, Book 9).

qa: Jesus says “I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf” (16:26). Doesn't he intercede for us?

He does: he “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25). In John 16 he is not denying this. He is saying that the disciples are not kept at a distance from the Father, as though only Jesus could speak to him. United with the Son, they themselves can go to the Father, who already loves them.
rite: St Ambrose (died 397) belongs to the Latin West, yet he read and drew on the Greek Fathers of the East. He is a reminder that East and West share one inheritance of faith. As a bishop who stood firm and also taught the newly baptized about the sacraments, he speaks to a Malankara Church in the middle of its fast: guard what you have received, and hand it on to the next generation in your homes and Sunday schools.
study: “I know the one in whom I have put my trust.” What do I need to entrust to him today?
Jesus promises peace in the middle of trouble, not after it. Where can I claim this promise this week?

lead: In the middle of the Suboro season, as the Church walks toward Yaldo, she stops to give thanks for the beginning of the woman through whom the Word took flesh. Neither of today's readings tells of the beginning of Mary's life. Scripture does not narrate it. They show instead why it matters. Paul gives the one line in his letters that touches the Mother of the Lord: “God sent his Son, born of a woman”. Luke gives us Mary's own voice, praising the God who “has done great things” for her.

Read together, the two passages explain the feast. Galatians says what God was preparing: a Son born under the law, so that slaves might become children. The Magnificat says how Mary understands her place in it: she calls God “my Savior”, and she gives all the credit to his mercy. The key words are fullness, adoption and mercy.

r.h: Born of a woman, so that we might be children
set: Paul wrote to the churches of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey, because teachers had come urging his Gentile converts to accept circumcision and the observance of the Mosaic law as necessary for salvation. Paul answers that faith in Christ has already made them children of God. Just before this passage he has said: “in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith” (3:26).

To explain this he uses an everyday legal picture. An heir who is still a child owns everything in principle, yet in practice he lives under others' orders until the date his father has set. That date, Paul says, has now come.
str: vv. 1–2: the picture: the young heir under guardians and trustees.
v. 3: the application: “while we were minors, we were enslaved”.
vv. 4–5: the turning point: God sends his Son, for a double purpose: to redeem and to make us children.
vv. 6–7: the proof: the Spirit in our hearts cries “Abba! Father!”

¶ Notice the pattern of the whole passage: God sends his Son (v. 4), and God sends the Spirit of his Son (v. 6). Father, Son and Spirit appear together, and all three are at work in making us children.
kw: Time is pictured as a vessel that God fills to the brim. The Son comes not by accident of history but at the date set by the Father, as in v. 2. The Catechism says that the Annunciation to Mary opens this fullness of time (CCC 484).

A Hebrew way of saying “a real human being” (compare Job 14:1). Paul does not name Mary and says nothing here about the manner of the birth. His point is that the Son is truly one of us. Even so, the Church has always heard in this phrase the place God gave to the woman from whom his Son took flesh.
A word from Greek and Roman law. An adopted child had the full rights of a child and heir. God does not merely release slaves; he brings them into the family.

The phrase is debated. It may mean the basic elements of the world, which people of that age often linked with spiritual powers, or the elementary rules of religion. In both cases it describes life before the coming of the Son as life under a kind of childhood bondage.
The Aramaic word for father, kept in Greek by the early Church because it was Jesus' own word in prayer (Mark 14:36; see also Romans 8:15).
vv: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,

“Sent” shows that the Son already existed before his birth. “Born of a woman” shows that he truly became man. The two phrases hold together the whole mystery of the Incarnation, and the second one is the reason we honour his Mother.
in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children.

He entered our condition so that we might enter his. The early Fathers often repeated this exchange: the Son of God became a son of man so that we might become children of God (so St Irenaeus and St Athanasius, in substance; see CCC 460).
And because you are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”
The Spirit prays within us with the same word the Son used. Every time a Christian says “Father”, that prayer is the work of the Spirit (CCC 683, 742).
So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if a child then also an heir, through God.
Paul moves from “we” to a singular “you”, as if speaking to each reader in turn. The last two words matter: this inheritance comes “through God”, as a gift and not as something earned.
ch: The Catechism quotes Galatians 4:4–5 at the opening of its teaching on Jesus Christ (CCC 422), and it teaches that God, preparing a body for his Son, wanted a creature's willing cooperation, and so chose a daughter of Israel (CCC 488). The doctrine proclaimed today says that this preparation reached back to the first moment of her existence: “by a singular grace and privilege of almighty God and by virtue of the merits of Jesus Christ, Savior of the human race”, Mary was preserved from all stain of original sin (Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus, 1854; CCC 491). St Irenaeus, comparing Eve and Mary, says that the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by Mary's obedience (CCC 494).

r.h: The Mighty One has done great things for me
set: Mary has travelled to the hill country of Judea to help her kinswoman Elizabeth. Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, has just called her “blessed” because she believed (1:42–45). The Magnificat is Mary's reply. She turns the praise away from herself and gives it to God.

The song is woven almost entirely from the Old Testament: above all the song of Hannah, the barren woman who became the mother of Samuel (1 Samuel 2:1–10), and also the Psalms. Mary speaks in the language of Israel's prayer. She stands among the poor of the Lord, whose hope she carries, and the Catechism calls her the purest figure among them (CCC 64).
str: vv. 46–49: Mary's own thanksgiving: what God has done for her.
v. 50: the bridge: his mercy for every generation.
vv. 51–53: what God does in history: the proud scattered, the lowly lifted up, the hungry filled.
vv. 54–55: God keeps his promise to Israel and to Abraham.
v. 56: the narrative close: three months with Elizabeth.
¶ The song moves outward, from one young woman to all generations, and then back to Abraham. What God has done in Mary is the pattern of what he does for all his people.
kw: From megas, great. To magnify the Lord is to declare him great. It adds nothing to God. It clears the soul to see him as he is. The Latin form of the word, Magnificat, gives the song its name.

It means a low condition, not only a humble feeling. It is the very word of Hannah's prayer in the Greek Old Testament, when she asks God to look on the “misery” of his servant (1 Samuel 1:11). Mary is not praising her own humility. She is saying that God looked down on someone small.

The word appears twice in the song (vv. 50, 54). It stands for the Hebrew ḥesed, God's faithful covenant love. The whole Magnificat rests on it, and so does the Immaculate Conception, which is a work of mercy and not a reward.
vv: And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,

Mary herself calls God “my Savior”. This line answers an old objection to today's feast. The Church does not teach that Mary had no need of a Saviour. She teaches that Mary was redeemed in a more exalted way, “by reason of the merits of her Son” (CCC 492; Lumen Gentium 53). A person can be rescued after falling into the pit, or be held back before reaching it; both owe their lives to the rescuer.
for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed;
This is a bold prophecy from a village girl, and the Church has kept it for two thousand years. Our honour to Mary is the fulfilment of her own words (CCC 971).
for the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
Here is the feast in one line. Everything in Mary is what the Mighty One has done. Her holiness is the work of a holy God.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty.

The Greek verbs are in the past tense. Mary speaks as if the reversal had already happened, because in the child she carries God has already begun it. St John Paul II wrote that the Church's love for the poor is inscribed in the Magnificat (Redemptoris Mater 37).
ch: The Catechism calls the Magnificat the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church (CCC 2619), and it holds up Mary's words as the model of adoration: to confess with gratitude that God has done great things, and that holy is his name (CCC 2097). St Ambrose, preaching on this passage, prays that the soul of Mary may be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and her spirit in each of us to rejoice in God (in substance). The Eastern Fathers call the Mother of God “the All-Holy”, as the Catechism recalls, “free from any stain of sin, as though fashioned by the Holy Spirit and formed as a new creature” (CCC 493; Lumen Gentium 56).

qa: Is the Immaculate Conception the same as the Virgin Birth?

No, though many people confuse them. Today's feast is about the beginning of Mary's own life: from the first moment she was preserved from original sin. Her parents, whom tradition names Joachim and Anne, conceived her in the ordinary way. The virginal conception concerns Jesus: he was conceived in Mary's womb by the power of the Holy Spirit, without a human father (CCC 490–491, 496–497).
Where is this in the Bible?

Scripture does not state it in so many words. The Church reads it in the light of God's promise of enmity between the serpent and the woman (Genesis 3:15; CCC 410–411), and of the angel's greeting: “Greetings, favored one” (Luke 1:28), where the Greek kecharitōmenē means one who has been and remains filled with grace (CCC 490–491). The dogma of 1854 expresses what the Church had come to understand slowly over the centuries, through prayer and reflection on Scripture.
Did Mary then not need Christ?

She needed him more than anyone, and she says so: “God my Savior”. She was redeemed by Christ, and in the most perfect way, by being preserved from sin instead of being cleansed from it (CCC 492). All her grace flows from his Cross.
rite: The West Syriac Fathers sang of the Mother of God, the Yoldath Aloho, long before the Latin definition. St Ephrem says to the Lord in one of his hymns that he and his Mother alone are entirely beautiful: there is no blemish in him, and no stain in his Mother (Nisibene Hymns 27, in substance). The Syro-Malankara Catholic reader therefore receives today's dogma, proclaimed in Rome, as a clear statement of a praise already sung in his own tradition. In the Suboro season the feast has a particular place: Suboro is the time of good news, and here the first good news is that God began to prepare a home for his Son long before the angel came to Nazareth. At the Holy Qurbono we receive the Body born of this pure Virgin, and with her our souls magnify the Lord.
study: Paul says God sent his Son “when the fullness of time had come”. Where have I seen God's timing prove better than my own?
How would I explain to a friend the difference between the Immaculate Conception and the virginal conception of Jesus?
Mary calls God “my Savior”. How does this help me to honour her without losing sight of Christ?
Whom does the Magnificat ask me to notice today: the lowly, the hungry, those without power?

lead: Both readings ask who Jesus is. Hebrews answers from the heights: he is the Son through whom God has spoken his last word. Luke answers from the road: John the Baptist, in prison, asks, “Are you the one who is to come?”, and Jesus points to what he is doing for the blind, the lame and the poor. The glory of the Son and his care for the lowly belong to one Person.

r.h: God has spoken to us by a Son
set: This single long and carefully built sentence in Greek opens the Letter to the Hebrews, a sermon written for tired Christians who were tempted to drift away. There is no greeting and no name of an author. The preacher begins with God speaking, and in four verses he says who Christ is before he says anything else.
str: vv. 1–2a: two times, two ways of speaking: long ago by the prophets, now by a Son.
vv. 2b–3: seven statements about the Son: heir, agent of creation, radiance of glory, imprint of God's being, sustainer of all, purifier from sin, seated at the right hand.
v. 4: he is greater than the angels, which the rest of the chapter will develop.
kw: Two rhythmic Greek adverbs: in many parts and in many manners. God's word in the prophets was true but given in pieces. The Son is not one more piece.
Brightness streaming out from a source of light. The Son is the light that shines from the Father, and is never apart from him, as the Creed says: “Light from Light” (CCC 241).

The mark a seal or a stamp leaves in wax or on a coin. The Son shows exactly what the Father is. The word translated “very being” is hypostasis, a term that later became important in the Church's teaching on the Trinity, though here it is not yet used in that later technical sense.
vv: Long ago God spoke to our ancestors in many and various ways by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son,
The Greek has no “the” here: literally “by a Son”. The contrast is between kinds of speakers. The prophets were servants who carried a message. This speaker is himself the message.
He is the reflection of God’s glory and the exact imprint of God’s very being, and he sustains all things by his powerful word.
The one who holds up the universe is also the one who “made purification for sins”. Then he “sat down”, because that work is finished.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses to teach that Christ is the Father's one, perfect and final Word (CCC 65). In the same paragraph it gives the words of St John of the Cross: in giving us his Son, God spoke everything to us at once, and he has no more to say. The Church expects no new public revelation before the Lord's return (CCC 66).

r.h: Are you the one who is to come?
set: Herod has shut John in prison (Luke 3:20). John's disciples tell him “all these things”: just before this, Jesus has healed a centurion's servant and raised a widow's son at Nain (7:1–17). John had announced a stronger one who would come with fire and a winnowing fork (3:16–17). What he now hears is mercy, and he sends two disciples to ask.
str: vv. 18–20: John's question, carried by two messengers.
v. 21: Jesus' answer begins in deeds.
vv. 22–23: the answer in words, with a beatitude at the end.
kw: the one who is to come
A way of speaking of the awaited one sent by God (compare Psalm 118:26; Malachi 3:1). John had used the same verb in 3:16.
To stumble over something placed in the path. Jesus knows that a Messiah of mercy, who leaves his herald in prison, can be a stumbling block for those who expect something else.
vv: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?”

Did John himself doubt? St John Chrysostom held that he asked for the sake of his disciples, to send them to Jesus (in substance). Many modern commentators think the question is John's own, the honest question of a faithful man in a dark prison. Either way, it is a question brought to the right person.
the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news brought to them.
Jesus does not say yes. He lets Isaiah answer (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5–6; 61:1). The list ends not with the raising of the dead but with the poor, as if that were the greatest sign.
And blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.
This is a gentle word for John, and a word for all whose prayers seem to bring no release.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the signs of Jesus show that the Kingdom is present in him and attest that he is the promised Messiah, and that they can also become an occasion of offense (CCC 547–548). They are not given to satisfy curiosity but to call to faith. Good news for the poor is a mark of the Kingdom (CCC 544).

study: Hebrews says God has spoken “by a Son”. How much of my day is shaped by listening to him?
What question would I send to Jesus from my own prison, and where might he be answering it already?

lead: Today the Syriac Churches remember Mar Behnam, his sister Sarah and the Forty Martyrs. The readings give two faces of Christian witness. In Thessalonica it is a quiet life of love, honest work and good standing with neighbours. In Matthew it is open confession before those who can kill the body. Jesus says “do not be afraid” because the Father knows the fall of every sparrow.

r.h: Taught by God to love one another
set: First Thessalonians is very probably the oldest surviving Christian writing, from about AD 50 or 51. Paul had to leave this young church in Macedonia in a hurry, and he writes with joy at the good report he has received. In chapter 4 he turns to how they should live. Some of them may have been neglecting ordinary work; he returns to this in 2 Thessalonians 3:6–12.
str: vv. 9–10a: on love: you have been taught by God, and you already practise it.
v. 10b: do so more and more.
vv. 11–12: live quietly, work, and depend on no one.
kw: love of the brothers and sisters
In the Greek world this word meant love between children of one family. Christians used it for the new family of faith.
This word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It recalls the promises of Isaiah 54:13 and Jeremiah 31:33–34, that in the new age God himself would teach his people.
Paul makes a small paradox. The verb “aspire” means to pursue honour eagerly. Here the honour to be pursued is quietness.
vv: you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another;
The law of love is written within them by the Spirit. Paul does not need to teach it; he only needs to remind them.
to aspire to live quietly, to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we directed you,
Paul himself worked night and day so as not to burden anyone (2:9). Greek society of his time often despised manual work. Here it becomes part of a Christian witness.
so that you may behave properly toward outsiders and be dependent on no one.
Love looks outward too: the neighbour who does not share the faith sees how Christians live.
ch: The Catechism says that work honours the Creator's gifts and that it can be a means of holiness, united to Christ the carpenter of Nazareth (CCC 2427). Love is the first gift of the Spirit, which no one can give himself. The martyrs we remember today did not begin with a great moment. They began, as we do, with daily faithfulness.

r.h: Do not be afraid
set: This passage belongs to the second of Jesus' five great discourses in Matthew, in which he sends out the Twelve (Matthew 10). He has just warned them of courts, floggings and hatred (10:17–25). Now the tone changes. Three times he says that they are not to fear (vv. 26, 28, 31). Matthew's first readers probably knew from experience what this meant.
str: vv. 26–27: do not fear, because the truth will come out: proclaim it.
v. 28: do not fear those who can only kill the body.
vv. 29–31: do not fear, for the Father cares even for sparrows.
vv. 32–33: acknowledge Jesus, and he will acknowledge you.
kw: From the Hebrew name for the valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, a place remembered for child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31; 2 Kings 23:10). It became an image of final ruin.
A small copper coin of little value. Two sparrows for one such coin: the cheapest living thing in the market.
To say the same thing, to declare openly, as one does in a court. It is the word for confession of faith.
vv: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
The one to be feared is God, not the devil. This is reverence, not terror, since the next verse speaks of this same God as “your Father”. Fear of God frees a person from every other fear.
Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
Jesus does not promise that the sparrow will not fall. He promises that it will not fall alone. This is a word for martyrs.
“Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven;
Our confession on earth and Christ's confession before the Father are joined. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473).
ch: The Catechism draws on verses like these when it teaches that God's care reaches the smallest things (CCC 302–305), and that Jesus' warnings about Gehenna are a call to responsibility and conversion (CCC 1034, 1036). The Church has always kept the memory of her martyrs, and she has read this chapter as being fulfilled in them.

rite: The tradition of the Syriac Churches tells that Mar Behnam and Sarah were children of a Persian ruler in the fourth century, that Behnam came to faith through the monk Mar Mattai, that Sarah was healed and baptised, and that they were put to death with forty companions. The story as we have it is partly legendary, and its details cannot be checked. What is certain is the long love of the Syriac faithful for these martyrs, witnessed by the ancient monastery that bears Mar Behnam's name near Mosul in northern Iraq. Christians of that land have suffered greatly in our own time, and today's Gospel may lead us to pray for them at the Holy Qurbono.
study: Which is harder for me today: the quiet faithfulness Paul describes, or open witness before others?
What fear is holding me back from acknowledging Christ, and what does the image of the sparrow say to it?

lead: At first sight the readings seem to be about small practical things: how to save money for a collection, and what may be done on a sabbath. In both, the Lord's day and mercy come together. Paul asks the Corinthians to set money aside for the poor “on the first day of every week”. Jesus defends his hungry disciples with the word of Hosea, “I desire mercy”.

r.h: The collection for the saints
set: Paul is ending his letter from Ephesus (16:8). One of the great projects of his life was a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28; 2 Corinthians 8–9; Galatians 2:10). It was relief for the hungry, and also a visible sign that Jew and Gentile were one Church in Christ.
str: v. 1: the same directions as for the churches of Galatia.
v. 2: the method: every week, each person, according to what he can save.
vv. 3–4: trustworthy carriers, approved by the church.
kw: A rare word in the New Testament, found only here (vv. 1–2). Elsewhere Paul prefers richer religious words for the same collection: fellowship, service, grace.
the first day of the week
The day of the Lord's resurrection (Mark 16:2; Acts 20:7). This verse is one of the earliest signs that Christians gave a special place to this day of the week.
In v. 3 the word for “your gift” is simply “grace”. The money is a grace that passes from God, through them, to the poor.
vv: On the first day of every week, each of you is to put aside and save whatever extra you earn, so that collections need not be taken when I come.
Regular and small, planned and not emotional. Each one gives; nobody is left out. Paul does not want people pressured at the last moment.
And when I arrive, I will send any whom you approve with letters to take your gift to Jerusalem.
Paul handles money with care. The church itself chooses the carriers and he gives them letters. Honesty in Church money is an old apostolic concern.
ch: The Catechism cites this passage when it says that from the very beginning Christians brought, along with the bread and wine for the Eucharist, gifts to share with those in need (CCC 1351). About a century after Paul, St Justin Martyr describes how the Sunday assembly collected gifts to help orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers (First Apology 67). Sunday worship and care for the poor have always gone together (CCC 2178, 2443–2449).

r.h: The Son of Man is lord of the sabbath
set: Just before this passage Jesus has said, “Come to me, all you that are weary… and I will give you rest” (11:28). Now the question of rest arises in practice. To pluck grain by hand from a neighbour's field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25). The objection is that it was done on the sabbath, when reaping was forbidden (Exodus 34:21). The Pharisees were not being petty: they were serious about guarding a holy day, which was God's gift and a sign of Israel's covenant. Such debates about what the sabbath allows were common among Jewish teachers of the time.
str: vv. 1–2: the disciples are hungry; the Pharisees object.
vv. 3–4: first argument: David and the bread of the Presence (1 Samuel 21:1–6).
vv. 5–6: second argument: priests work in the Temple on the sabbath (Numbers 28:9–10); “something greater than the temple is here”.
v. 7: the key: Hosea 6:6.
v. 8: the claim: the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
kw: In Hosea 6:6 this stands for the Hebrew ḥesed, loyal love. Matthew alone has Jesus quote this verse, and he does so twice (9:13; 12:7).
The word is neuter, “something greater”. It can point to Jesus' own person, or to the Kingdom present in him. Either way, a claim of this size goes far beyond an argument about grain.
vv: I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.
If Temple service permits work on the sabbath, how much more does service to the one who is greater than the Temple?
But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless.
Hosea does not reject sacrifice. It is a Hebrew way of saying “this first, and that only with it”. Worship without mercy is empty.
For the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
Jesus claims the authority of the one who gave the sabbath. He does not abolish the day. He teaches its true meaning.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus never failed to respect the holiness of the sabbath, and gave its law its authentic and authoritative interpretation (CCC 2173). It also cautions against the idea that Jesus simply opposed the Pharisees: his relations with them were not only polemical, and he had much in common with them (CCC 575–576, 579). It uses the same word of Hosea to teach that outward sacrifice must express the heart (CCC 2100). The Christian Sunday keeps this spirit: it is a day for God, for rest, and for works of mercy (CCC 2185–2186).

qa: Do Christians have to keep the sabbath?

The Christian keeps the Lord's Day, Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, which fulfils the spiritual truth of the sabbath (CCC 2175–2176). The commandment remains, and it is lived on the day of the new creation.
study: Paul asks for a small, regular amount set aside weekly. What would it mean for my family to plan our giving in this way?
Where might I be defending a rule while forgetting the person who is hungry?

lead: Two teachers speak to two communities about how to live together. Paul gives the Thessalonians a run of short commands: respect your leaders, help the weak, rejoice, pray, give thanks. Jesus speaks more sharply to his disciples: do not trip up the little ones, and cut away what makes you fall. Both end in the same place: peace among yourselves.

r.h: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing
set: These are the closing instructions of Paul's letter. The young church has been told to watch for the Lord's coming (5:1–11). Now Paul explains what watching looks like day by day: it is a life of mutual care in the community. The commands come quickly and short, probably so that they could be easily remembered when the letter was read aloud.
str: vv. 12–13: respect for those who lead.
vv. 14–15: care for one another: the idle, the fainthearted, the weak.
vv. 16–18: three short commands about prayer.
vv. 19–22: discernment: neither quench nor swallow everything.
kw: Literally those who stand in front, who lead and care. This is an early glimpse of pastoral leadership in the Church, before the later titles became fixed.
A word for what goes on without a break. It means prayer that keeps returning, not words without a pause.
The word used for assaying metal. Spiritual gifts are to be welcomed and also tested. “Test everything” is about prophecy, not doubting all things.
vv: And we urge you, beloved, to admonish the idlers, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all of them.
Different people need different care: one needs correction, another courage, another a helping hand. Patience is for everyone.
Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.

Paul wrote “in all circumstances”, not “for all circumstances”. He had suffered at Philippi and been driven out of Thessalonica. The verb “give thanks” is eucharisteite, from which the word Eucharist comes.
Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise the words of prophets, but test everything; hold fast to what is good;
The Spirit is compared to a fire that can be put out. The Church must neither stifle the Spirit nor accept everything that claims to come from him.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses in its teaching on persevering prayer (CCC 2742) and on thanksgiving: every event and need can become an offering of thanks (CCC 2638). St Augustine, preaching on the Psalms, says that your desire is your prayer, and if your desire is continuous, your prayer is continuous (in substance). The Syriac daily office, with its hours of prayer through the day and night, is one way the Church has tried to live this command.

r.h: Have salt in yourselves
set: Jesus and the disciples are in a house at Capernaum. On the road the disciples have been arguing about who is the greatest (9:33–34). Jesus has placed a child among them (9:36) and has defended an outsider who cast out demons in his name (9:38–41). Now he turns to the harm that believers can do, and to the harm they do themselves.
str: v. 42: do not cause a little one to stumble.
vv. 43–48: three sayings: hand, foot, eye.
vv. 49–50: sayings linked by the word salt, ending in peace.
