¶ A note on the text: the oldest manuscripts have no separate vv. 44 and 46, which repeat v. 48 in later copies, so the NRSV passes over those numbers. The POC keeps the numbers by dividing vv. 43 and 45 into two verses each, and it also divides vv. 47–48 differently. The verse numbers therefore do not line up exactly in the two versions.
kw: From skandalon, a trap or an obstacle in the path. It is the key word of the passage, appearing four times (vv. 42, 43, 45, 47). It means leading someone into sin or away from faith.
Literally a “donkey millstone”, the great upper stone of a mill turned by an animal, not the small hand mill. The image is deliberately terrible.
Salt preserves, purifies and gives flavour. It was added to sacrifices (Leviticus 2:13) and is linked with covenant (Numbers 18:19). Sharing salt was a sign of fellowship.
vv: “If any of you put a stumbling block before one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for you if a great millstone were hung around your neck and you were thrown into the sea.
“Little ones” means vulnerable believers, not only children. Jesus' strongest language is kept for those who damage the faith of the weak.
If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off; it is better for you to enter life maimed than to have two hands and to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire.
This is deliberate exaggeration in the Semitic manner. It does not ask for injury to the body. It asks for a decisive break with whatever leads to sin.
Salt is good; but if salt has lost its saltiness, how can you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.

The words “salted with fire” (v. 49) are hard. They probably mean that everyone will be tested and purified, as a sacrifice is salted, and some later manuscripts add a line from Leviticus to explain this. The last word goes back to the argument on the road: peace, not rank.
ch: The Catechism teaches that scandal is a grave offence when it leads another to sin, and that it is especially grave when it comes from those in authority or harms the weak (CCC 2284–2287). The sharp sayings about hand and eye call for the conversion of the heart. They have never been understood by the Church as a command to harm the body (see CCC 2297).

qa: Why does the POC have verses 44 and 46 when the English does not?

The difference is only in the numbering, not in the teaching. Some later copies repeat the line about the worm and the fire after vv. 43 and 45, and these repeats were numbered 44 and 46. The oldest manuscripts do not have them, so the NRSV passes over those numbers. The POC does not have the repeat either; it divides vv. 43 and 45 into two verses each, so that the numbers stay in place.
study: Who in my community needs correction, who needs courage, and who needs a hand today? Which of these do I find hardest to give?
Is there a habit, a place or a screen that I need to cut away, before it costs me more?

lead: On this Suboro Sunday the good news comes to a carpenter, in his sleep. Matthew tells of the birth of Jesus from Joseph's side. The evening Gospel and the Gospel of the Holy Qurbono are the same passage (Matthew 1:18–25), and the other readings gather around it. Sirach 7 teaches humility and fidelity. In 1 Samuel 3 the boy Samuel says, “Speak, for your servant is listening”, and receives a hard word without hiding it. In Isaiah 45 God calls all the ends of the earth to turn to him and be saved. In 1 Peter 2 believers are told to live honourably among the nations.

This study takes three of them. In Genesis 37 another Joseph dreams, and the dream costs him everything before it saves his family. In Galatians 1 Paul tells how God called him through grace and revealed his Son to him. In Matthew 1 the just man wakes up and does what he was told. All three are about a call from God that comes unasked and that overturns a person's plans. The key words are dream, call and obedience.

r.h: The dreams of Joseph, son of Jacob
set: The long story of Joseph (Genesis 37–50) explains how the family of Jacob came to Egypt. It opens with a family already in trouble. Joseph is seventeen, the son of his father's old age, loved more than his brothers, and he has brought their father a bad report about them (37:2–4). His brothers cannot speak peaceably to him. Into this tension come two dreams.

In the ancient Near East dreams were commonly taken as a way God might make his will known. In Genesis, God does not speak directly to Joseph as he spoke to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He guides events through dreams and through the hidden course of the story, as Joseph himself will say at the end (45:5; 50:20).
str: vv. 5–8: the first dream: the sheaves bow; the brothers hate him more.
vv. 9–10: the second dream: sun, moon and eleven stars bow; his father rebukes him.
v. 11: the two responses: the brothers' jealousy, and the father's keeping the matter.
¶ The sheaves look forward to the famine years, when grain in Egypt will bring these same brothers to bow before Joseph (42:6). The dream, which starts all the trouble, is also what God fulfils.
kw: The word is repeated through the passage. Joseph's story is told in three pairs of dreams: his own two, those of the butler and baker, and those of Pharaoh.
The word for homage to a king and for worship of God. It appears in both dreams, and it is the very thing the brothers cannot bear.
The basic meaning is to guard or to keep. In v. 11 Jacob “kept the matter in mind”. He has rebuked his son, and yet he does not dismiss the dream.
vv: Once Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him even more.
The text does not call Joseph blameless. A favourite son telling such dreams is not being wise. God works through a young man who still has much to learn in a pit and a prison.
“What kind of dream is this that you have had? Shall we indeed come, I and your mother and your brothers, and bow to the ground before you?”

Rachel's death has already been told (35:19). The story here does not stop over this, and interpreters explain it in different ways: perhaps “your mother” means Leah or whoever held the mother's place in the household, or the narrative is not arranged strictly in time. The moon in the dream stands for the mother in any case.
So his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.
Readers of Luke will recall Mary, who “treasured all these words” (Luke 2:19, 51). There are those who hate what God is doing, and those who hold on to it without yet understanding.
ch: The Catechism cites the story of Joseph to show how God, in his providence, can bring good even out of evil: “It was not you who sent me here, but God” (CCC 312). The Fathers saw in Joseph a figure of Christ: beloved of his father, sold by his own, and saving those who had rejected him; St Ambrose wrote a whole work on him. St Bernard compares the two Josephs: the first stored grain for Egypt, and the second kept safe the Bread from heaven for the whole world (in substance).

r.h: Called through his grace
set: Paul is under attack in Galatia. Some have been saying that his gospel is a second-hand and watered-down version of what he learned from the leaders in Jerusalem. He answers with his own story. It is one of the fullest pieces of autobiography in his letters, and it gives us precious dates and places for the years after his call.
str: vv. 11–12: the thesis: my gospel came by revelation of Jesus Christ.
vv. 13–14: my earlier life: a persecutor and a zealous Jew.
vv. 15–17: God's call, then Arabia and Damascus.
vv. 18–20: after three years, fifteen days with Cephas in Jerusalem.
vv. 21–24: Syria and Cilicia; the churches of Judea glorify God.
kw: An unveiling. In v. 12 it may mean a revelation from Jesus Christ or about him, and v. 16 suggests both: God “was pleased to reveal his Son to me”. The Greek en emoi there is literally “in me”, so the revelation is both to him and within him.
Paul's words about being set apart before birth echo the call of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5) and of the Servant (Isaiah 49:1). He sees his call as a prophet's call, and not as a change of God.

In the New Testament this word occurs only here (vv. 13–14). It means the Jewish way of life, zealously practised. Paul does not speak of leaving his God. The God who called him is the God of his ancestors.
The verb in v. 18, used only here in the New Testament. It suggests a visit made to get to know someone and to learn from him, as a visitor comes to see a person of importance.
vv: I was violently persecuting the church of God and was trying to destroy it.
Paul never hides this (1 Corinthians 15:9). The worst thing about him becomes the proof of grace.
But when God, who had set me apart before I was born and called me through his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles,
Every word places the initiative with God: he set apart, he called, he was pleased, he revealed. And the call has a purpose: it is for others.
Then after three years I did go up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and stayed with him fifteen days;

Paul stresses his independence, and yet he goes to Peter, using his Aramaic name, “Cephas”. Revelation does not make him a private Christian. He will go up again later and lay his gospel before the leaders “in order to make sure that I was not running, or had not run, in vain” (2:2).
And they glorified God because of me.
The persecutor's life has become a reason for others to praise God.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches that faith in Jesus as Son of God is at the centre of Paul's preaching: from the start, his call was the revealing of the Son (CCC 442). Paul also says that he handed on what he had received (1 Corinthians 15:3). The Church holds these together: the gospel comes from God and not from men, and it is kept and handed on in the communion of the apostles (CCC 75–77). It belongs among the Sunday's readings because of the word “called”: like Joseph, Paul has his plans overturned by God.

r.h: Joseph did as the angel commanded
set: Matthew has just given the genealogy of Jesus, which ends strangely: “Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born” (1:16). He has not said “Joseph the father of Jesus”. Today's passage explains why. The question is how Jesus, who has no human father, can be the son of David. The answer lies with Joseph's obedience.

A Jewish betrothal of that time was far more binding than an engagement today. The couple were legally husband and wife, and only a divorce could end it, though they did not yet live together. So Matthew calls Joseph “her husband” even at this stage. A woman found with child in this situation faced public shame, and the law spoke of severe penalties (Deuteronomy 22:20–27).
str: v. 18: the situation: found with child, from the Holy Spirit.
v. 19: Joseph's decision.
vv. 20–21: the angel's word in a dream: take her, and name him.
vv. 22–23: the fulfilment of Isaiah 7:14.
vv. 24–25: Joseph does exactly what he was told.

¶ Joseph does not say a word, here or anywhere in the Gospels. Matthew's account is built around what he does: he plans, he wakes, he takes, he names. Matthew's account of the childhood will repeat this pattern (2:13–15, 19–23).
kw: A just man in the Bible is one who lives by God's law. Joseph's justice appears in a surprising way: he will not expose her. In him justice and mercy are not in conflict.
The Hebrew name means “the Lord saves” (CCC 430, 452). The angel gives the explanation himself: “he will save his people from their sins”.
A title that Matthew otherwise keeps for Jesus. By naming the child, Joseph accepts him as his own in law, and through Joseph Jesus enters the line of David (CCC 437).

From Isaiah 7:14. The Hebrew has ‘almāh, young woman; the Greek Old Testament, which Matthew quotes, has parthenos, virgin. Matthew's Gospel begins with “God is with us” and ends with Jesus' own promise, “I am with you always” (28:20).
vv: Her husband Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.

St John Chrysostom admires the gentleness of Joseph, who wished to hide the matter and not to punish (in substance). This is the moment before the angel: a good man doing the best he can see, in the dark.
“Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.
“Do not be afraid” is the word of this whole season. God does not remove Joseph from the difficulty. He gives him a new part in it.
She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”
Naming was the father's right and task. God gives this legal fatherhood to a man who did not beget the child. It is real fatherhood, in care and in law.
When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him; he took her as his wife,
No delay and no conditions. St John Paul II says that what Joseph did is the clearest “obedience of faith”, and that in this he was joined to the faith of Mary (Redemptoris Custos 4).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Joseph was called by God to take Mary as his wife, so that Jesus should be born of Joseph's spouse into the messianic lineage of David (CCC 437). It reads the angel's words as the heart of the Gospel: the revelation of God's mercy to sinners (CCC 1846). The Gospel understands the virginal conception as a divine work, beyond human understanding and possibility (CCC 497). St John Paul II calls Joseph the guardian of the Redeemer (Redemptoris Custos, 1989), and Pope Francis speaks of him as a father in the shadows (Patris Corde, 2020).

qa: Did Joseph suspect Mary of sin?

Matthew does not say what he thought. Many readers, ancient and modern, take it that he knew only that she was with child, and did not know how, and that he chose not to expose her. Others in the tradition suggest that Joseph, sensing that something holy was happening, felt unworthy and meant to withdraw out of reverence. The text allows both. It tells us plainly only that he was just and that he did not want to shame her.
Does “until she had borne a son” mean that they lived as a married couple afterwards?

No. The Greek heōs, until, states what happened up to a point, and says nothing about what came after. St Jerome argued this at length against Helvidius, citing many biblical examples (in substance). Matthew's concern here is that Joseph was not the child's natural father. The Church confesses Mary as ever virgin (CCC 499–501).
Paul speaks of “James the Lord's brother”. Did Jesus have brothers?

Semitic languages had no separate common word for a cousin or other near relative, and the Bible often uses “brother” in a wide sense (see Genesis 13:8). The Church does not read these passages as speaking of other children of Mary (CCC 500). Many Eastern Fathers took them as children of Joseph by an earlier marriage, while St Jerome took them as cousins.
rite: The Sunday of the Apparition to St Joseph is one of the Suboro Sundays, which walk us step by step toward Yaldo: the announcement to Zechariah, the announcement to Mary, the visit to Elizabeth, the birth of John, and now the angel in Joseph's dream. Only with today's reading has the good news reached everyone who will share the home at Nazareth. The Malankara faithful, who are used to the long patience of the Syriac office, may find Joseph a friend in prayer: he has no recorded words, only a listening heart. At the Holy Qurbono we receive Christ under the humble signs of bread and wine, and we are asked for Joseph's kind of faith, which takes home what God gives without needing to understand all of it first.
study: Joseph had already made a decision when God spoke. When have I had to let God change a good plan of mine?
Jacob “kept the matter in mind” and Joseph “did as the angel commanded”. Which do I need more at present: patience with what I do not understand, or prompt obedience to what I do?
Paul says that God “set me apart before I was born”. How does it change my view of my life to think this is true of me too?
Where in my family or parish is the “quiet” justice of Joseph needed, a justice that refuses to expose or shame anyone?

lead: Today the Church remembers St John of the Cross, and the readings suit him. Hebrews lifts our eyes to Melchizedek, a priest without beginning or end, and through him to Christ. Luke brings us down to the road, where Jesus tells the crowd plainly what following him will cost. The eternal Priest is the one who walks to Jerusalem carrying the cross, and he invites us to carry ours.

r.h: Melchizedek, priest forever
set: The preacher has been working toward this passage since 5:6, 10 and 6:20. How can Jesus be a priest, when he comes from the tribe of Judah and not of Levi (7:14)? The answer is in Psalm 110:4: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”. To explain that verse he goes back to the only story about this man: Genesis 14:17–20. Melchizedek appears for a few verses, meets Abraham, blesses him, receives a tenth, and goes.
str: vv. 1–3: who Melchizedek was: his name, his city, and what Genesis leaves unsaid.
vv. 4–7: he is greater than Abraham, because he receives tithes from him and blesses him.
vv. 8–10: so he is greater than Levi too, who in a sense paid tithes in Abraham.
kw: The Hebrew name, as v. 2 explains it. Salem, usually taken to be Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2), sounds like šālôm, peace. The preacher reads the order as significant: first righteousness, then peace.
without father, without mother, without genealogy

Priests of Israel had to prove their descent (Ezra 2:61–63). Genesis gives no ancestors for Melchizedek. The preacher, using a method common among Jewish teachers of his time, reads this silence as a sign. He is not saying that Melchizedek had no parents.
Melchizedek is made to resemble the Son, not the other way round. The Son is the original; the figure in Genesis is the shadow.
vv: Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.
A priesthood that does not depend on descent, and that has no end: this is what Hebrews sees in Christ, who holds his priesthood permanently because he lives forever (7:24).
It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.
In the ancient world, the one who blessed stood higher than the one who received the blessing. Abraham, who carries all the promises, receives this stranger's blessing.
In the one case, tithes are received by those who are mortal; in the other, by one of whom it is testified that he lives.
“He lives” is the key of the argument. For the reader of Hebrews, it is true fully only of the risen Christ.
ch: Hebrews does not mention the bread and wine of Genesis 14:18, but the Church has seen them too. St Cyprian saw in Melchizedek's offering a figure of the Lord's sacrifice (in substance, Letter 63). The Catechism sees Melchizedek as a prefiguration of the priesthood of Christ, the unique “high priest after the order of Melchizedek” (CCC 1544), and sees the bread and wine he brought as a prefiguration of the Church's own offering (CCC 1333).

r.h: Carry the cross and count the cost
set: Jesus has set his face toward Jerusalem (9:51). Large crowds are walking with him, and he has just told the parable of the great dinner, where the house is filled with the poor and the lame (14:15–24). The invitation is open to everyone. Now he turns around and tells them what the invitation means.
str: vv. 25–27: two conditions: to love him above all, and to carry the cross.
vv. 28–32: two short parables: the tower and the king at war.
v. 33: the application: give up all.
vv. 34–35: the warning of the salt that has lost its taste.
kw: A Semitic idiom of preference: to put one thing decidedly second. Genesis 29:31 says Leah was “unloved”, literally “hated”, when in fact she was simply loved less than Rachel (29:30). Matthew 10:37 gives the sense: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me”.
To count with pebbles, as on a counting board. Discipleship is not to be entered on an impulse.
It also means to say farewell, to take one's leave. Discipleship includes a real letting go of what we hold.
vv: Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
Luke's readers knew what it looked like when a condemned man carried a cross through the streets. The Greek speaks of “his own” cross: each disciple has one, and no one can choose another's.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost, to see whether he has enough to complete it?
The surprise of the two parables is that Jesus does not ask for great enthusiasm. He asks for a clear head. He wants to have disciples who will finish.
So therefore, none of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.
The form of this will differ from one vocation to another. The inner freedom it asks for applies to all. The Catechism uses this verse to teach poverty of heart for every believer (CCC 2544).
“Salt is good; but if salt has lost its taste, how can its saltiness be restored?

According to a common explanation, Dead Sea salt was mixed with other minerals; when the true salt was washed out, a useless white residue remained. The Greek word for losing its taste also means to become foolish: a disciple who has lost his saltiness has lost his wisdom.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544), and that he calls them to take up their cross and follow him, because he wishes to associate with his redeeming sacrifice those who are to benefit from it (CCC 618). The Church has never understood this as a contempt for family. The same Lord commands us to honour our parents (CCC 2214–2218). It means that family, like everything else, is loved rightly when Christ comes first (CCC 2232).

qa: Does Jesus really want us to hate our parents?

No. “Hate” here is a Semitic way of saying “put second”, as Matthew 10:37 shows. Christ asks for the first place in our hearts, and he also commands love for parents and even for enemies. The saying is meant to shock us into seeing how serious the choice is.
rite: St John of the Cross (1542–1591), a Spanish Carmelite priest and Doctor of the Church, worked with St Teresa of Avila for the reform of Carmel. His own brothers in the order imprisoned him at Toledo, and there, in a dark cell, he began the poetry of the Spiritual Canticle. His teaching on the “nothing” (nada) that leaves room for the “all” of God is a commentary on today's Gospel. He belongs to the Latin tradition, and Syriac monastic readers will recognise in him the same call to stripping and interior silence that their own Fathers taught.
study: Hebrews reads Christ's priesthood in a figure who appears only for a moment in Genesis. How does this change the way I listen to the Old Testament at the Holy Qurbono?
If I sit down and honestly “estimate the cost”, what is following Christ asking of me at this time in my life?

lead: The Twenty-Five Days' Fast before Yaldo continues, and both readings look straight at what the world would call failure. Paul arrives in Corinth trembling, with nothing to offer but a crucified Lord. Jesus tells his friends that they will be put out and even killed. Together they teach that God's work does not rest on eloquence or success, a good lesson for those preparing to welcome a child born far from any palace.

r.h: Jesus Christ, and him crucified
set: Corinth was a busy Roman colony and port city on the isthmus of Greece, refounded by Julius Caesar in 44 BC. Paul preached there for a year and a half around AD 50–52 (Acts 18:1–11) and wrote this letter a few years later from Ephesus (16:8). The community had split into parties around favourite teachers (1:10–12), and many admired fine speech, as Greek city culture did. Paul had just said that “we proclaim Christ crucified” (1:23). Now he reminds them how he first came to them.
str: vv. 1–2: what Paul refused to bring, and the one thing he decided to bring.
vv. 3–4: his weakness, and the Spirit's power at work in it.
v. 5: the purpose: a faith that rests on God.
kw: The Greek perfect participle speaks of a past act whose effect remains. The risen Lord is still the one who was crucified; the Cross is never left behind.
A word used in Greek rhetoric for a compelling proof. Paul takes the orators' own word and gives it to the Holy Spirit: the proof is what God did in the Corinthians themselves.
vv: I did not come proclaiming the mystery of God to you in lofty words or wisdom.

A note on the text. The Greek manuscripts differ here: some read “mystery”, which the NRSV follows, and others read “testimony”, which the Malayalam POC follows. Both are ancient, and the sense is close: Paul came to pass on what God has done, not to display himself.
For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
This was a decision, not a lack of ability. Crucifixion was the most shameful death the Roman world knew, and Paul chooses it as his whole subject.
And I came to you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling.
The great apostle was afraid. Acts tells that the Lord had to encourage him in a night vision at Corinth: “Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent” (Acts 18:9).
so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God.
A faith that rests on a clever preacher will fall with him. A faith that rests on God can survive any preacher.
ch: The Catechism says that God's power is shown in the weakness of the Cross, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (CCC 272, quoting 1 Corinthians 1:24–25). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, keeps returning to one argument: unlearned men won the world, so the victory belongs to God (in substance). St John Paul II reads these chapters in Fides et Ratio 23: the word of the Cross does not abolish reason, but no human wisdom could have reached it by itself.

r.h: That you may not stumble
set: Jesus is speaking at the Last Supper (John 13–17). He has just warned that the world will hate his disciples as it hated him: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you” (15:20). The Fourth Gospel took its final form late in the first century, and many scholars think that some of its readers were Christians of Jewish birth who had painfully lost their place in the synagogue, the community of their childhood.
str: v. 1: the purpose of the warning.
vv. 2–3: what is coming, and its root: not knowing the Father.
v. 4: remember that I told you.
kw: From skandalon, a trap or an obstacle in the road. Jesus warns them in advance so that persecution will not trip up their faith.
This word occurs in the New Testament only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). It describes a real family and religious wound, not an abstract dispute.
The word for sacred service to God. The tragedy of v. 2 is that violence can be mistaken for worship.
vv: “I have said these things to you to keep you from stumbling.
Jesus does not promise an easy road. He gives something better: the truth in advance.
an hour is coming when those who kill you will think that by doing so they are offering worship to God.

Paul knew this from the inside: “I was violently persecuting the church of God” (Galatians 1:13). Religious zeal without knowledge of the Father can do terrible things. This warning has been true of Christians too, and every believer must take it to heart.
But I have said these things to you so that when their hour comes you may remember that I told you about them.
Remembering is the disciple's defence. The suffering that Jesus foretold cannot prove that he has lost control.
ch: The Catechism calls martyrdom “the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith” (CCC 2473). Tertullian told the Roman authorities that the blood of Christians is seed (Apology 50, in substance). The Church has seen this word come true in every age. In our own time, in many lands and in India too, some have suffered for their faith; we pray for them and, as the Lord taught, for those who wronged them.

qa: Does this passage blame the Jewish people?

No. Jesus and his first disciples were themselves Jews, and “they” here means those who would expel and persecute in that setting, not a whole people. The Church teaches that the Jews are not to be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4; see CCC 597–598).
study: Paul came to Corinth in fear and trembling. What work for God have I avoided because I felt too weak for it?
Have I ever defended my faith, or my community, in a way that hurt others? What would it mean to know the Father more truly in that situation?

lead: Paul asks three times to have his thorn removed and hears, “My grace is sufficient for you.” Jesus, after praying alone, asks, “But who do you say that I am?” The Epistle teaches us how to live with what God does not take away; the Gospel teaches us who it is that we are trusting. In the fast before Yaldo we learn that the One who comes in the weakness of a child is the Anointed of God.

r.h: My grace is sufficient for you
set: In 2 Corinthians 10–13 Paul defends himself against rivals who boasted of their gifts and mocked him: “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible” (10:10). Forced to boast, he lists his sufferings (11:23–33) and then speaks, with great reserve, of being caught up to “the third heaven” (12:2). Today's verses are the answer to that vision: what God gave Paul to keep him humble.
str: v. 7: the thorn and its purpose.
v. 8: three prayers.
v. 9a: the Lord's answer, the heart of the passage.
vv. 9b–10: Paul's new way of boasting.
kw: A sharp stake or splinter. Paul does not say what it was, and no one now knows. It may be meant to stay unnamed, so that every sufferer can recognise something of his own in it.
The verb is in the present tense: my grace is enough now, and it goes on being enough. Paul receives no explanation, only a promise.
to dwell, literally to pitch a tent upon

The “dwell” of v. 9. It is built on the Greek word for a tent, as is the verb in John 1:14, “lived among us”. The power of Christ comes and camps in a weak man. This is a fitting word for the days before Yaldo.
vv: a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, to keep me from being too elated.

“Was given” suggests that God is the giver, though Satan is the tormentor. Even the enemy's work is turned to serve God's purpose. St John Chrysostom took the thorn to mean Paul's human opponents (in substance); others have proposed an illness or a recurring temptation. The text does not settle it.
Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me,
Paul prayed as Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, more than once for the same thing (Matthew 26:44). Asking again is not a lack of faith.
“My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.”
God does say “no”, but this “no” contains a better gift. The answer to the prayer was not the removal of the thorn, but the presence of Christ.
for whenever I am weak, then I am strong.
This does not praise weakness for its own sake. It says that when our own resources run out, we finally have room for his.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse in two places: faith “glories in its weaknesses in order to draw to itself Christ's power” (CCC 273), and Paul had to learn that even the most intense prayers do not always obtain healing (CCC 1508). The second is especially comforting to the sick and to those who pray for them.

r.h: Who do you say that I am?
set: Luke places this scene right after the feeding of the five thousand (9:10–17). Earlier in the chapter Herod had asked, “who is this about whom I hear such things?” (9:9), and had heard the same three opinions: John, Elijah, an old prophet. Mark sets the same question near Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27). Luke omits the place and tells us something else instead: Jesus was praying.
str: v. 18: Jesus at prayer, and the first question.
v. 19: the opinion of the crowds.
v. 20: the second question and Peter's answer.
kw: The Greek for the Hebrew māšîaḥ: the king anointed by God for whom Israel hoped.
This form is special to Luke. The same title comes back at the Cross, on the lips of those who mock him (23:35). The title Peter speaks in faith will be fulfilled in a way he does not yet imagine.
vv: Once when Jesus was praying alone, with only the disciples near him, he asked them,
Luke often shows Jesus praying before decisive moments (3:21; 6:12; 9:28). This confession is born in the atmosphere of his prayer.
“But who do you say that I am?”
In Greek “you” comes first and is emphatic. Reports about other people's opinions are not enough; each disciple must answer in person.
Peter answered, “The Messiah of God.”
The answer is right, but incomplete. Jesus at once adds that the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and be raised (9:21–22).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus accepted Peter's confession and at once announced the coming Passion, which gives the title its true meaning (CCC 440). It also notes that in Luke Jesus prays before the decisive moments of his mission (CCC 2600). The Church's answer to the question is the Creed, which we confess at every Holy Qurbono.

study: What is my thorn? Have I been able to hear “My grace is sufficient for you” in it?
If Jesus asked me today, “But who do you say that I am?”, what would I say in my own words?

lead: The Church today remembers Mar Rabbula, Bishop of Edessa, while the fast before Yaldo continues. Both readings ask a pastoral question: how does a community tell true teaching from false? Paul says to watch those who divide and flatter. Jesus says to look at the fruit. And behind both stands a promise older than either of them: the serpent's head will be crushed.

r.h: The God of peace will crush Satan
set: Romans ends with a long list of greetings (16:1–16), full of warmth and names. Today's warning breaks into it rather suddenly. Paul has not yet visited Rome, and he does not name these people or say what they taught. He writes as a pastor who has seen elsewhere what such people can do to a community.
str: vv. 17–18: watch out for the dividers, and how to recognise them.
v. 19: Paul's joy and his wish for the Romans.
v. 20: the promise and the blessing.
kw: The POC keeps the literal word, “bellies”. Compare Philippians 3:19, “their god is the belly”. Paul means people who serve themselves, whether their appetite is for food, status or money.
Pleasant, plausible speech. Paul is not against kindness in speech; he warns against kindness used as a tool.
Literally “unmixed”, as of pure wine or metal. The same word is used in Matthew 10:16: “wise as serpents and innocent as doves”.
vv: keep an eye on those who cause dissensions and offenses, in opposition to the teaching that you have learned; avoid them.
The test is “the teaching that you have learned”: the faith already received. Paul is not asking the Romans to avoid everyone who asks a hard question.
I want you to be wise in what is good and guileless in what is evil.
A Christian is not asked to be naive. We should be sharp about what is good and have no skill in evil.
The God of peace will shortly crush Satan under your feet.

Note who is called what: the God of peace does the crushing. The dividers are defeated by the God who makes peace. The image echoes Genesis 3:15: “he will strike your head”. Paul adds that this victory will happen under your feet: Christ shares it with his Church.
ch: The Catechism calls Genesis 3:15 the Protoevangelium, the first announcement of the Messiah and of his victory, and notes that Christian tradition sees in it the New Adam and the woman who is his mother (CCC 410–411). St Irenaeus reads Genesis 3:15 as fulfilled in Christ, born of a woman, who overcomes the enemy (in substance). The Church reads this in the days before Yaldo for a good reason: the Child is the one promised at the beginning.

r.h: You will know them by their fruits
set: These verses come near the end of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). Jesus has spoken of the narrow gate (7:13–14). Now he warns of those who can lead people to the wrong one. Israel already knew the problem of false prophets (Deuteronomy 13; 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23). Matthew's Church apparently knew it too, as the next verses show (7:21–23).
str: v. 15: the warning: sheep outside, wolves inside.
v. 16a: the test.
vv. 16b–19: the images from farming.
v. 20: the test again, closing the passage.
kw: People who claim to speak for God without having been sent. The danger is that they look like members of the flock.
In the Bible this means what a life really produces. See Paul's list in Galatians 5:22–23.
vv: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.
Costume is the problem. Paul warned the elders of Ephesus about wolves too, from outside and from among themselves (Acts 20:29–30).
You will know them by their fruits.
The test does not depend on eloquence, miracles or popularity. It takes time, as fruit does. The sentence opens and closes this little passage (v. 20), so that we cannot miss it.
Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
Word for word, this is what John the Baptist preached in the desert (3:10). Jesus and his forerunner speak with one voice.
ch: An early Christian manual, the Didache, gives the same test: not everyone who speaks in the Spirit is a prophet, but only one who has the ways of the Lord (11:8, in substance). The Catechism takes “you will know them by their fruits” as a sign that grace is at work in a life (CCC 2005), and lists the fruits of the Spirit (CCC 1832). The test is therefore for us as well as for our teachers.

qa: Should I judge my pastors and teachers by this passage?

Jesus warned against a judging spirit (7:1), yet he also asks us to discern. The Church gives the standard: the faith handed down, the communion of the Church, and a life that bears the Spirit's fruit. Discernment should be humble and patient, and it should begin with our own tree.
rite: Mar Rabbula was Bishop of Edessa from about 411 until his death around 436, a central figure of the Syriac-speaking Church in his time. Syriac sources remember his strict discipline and his care for the poor and the sick. After the Council of Ephesus (431) he stood with St Cyril of Alexandria in defending the faith about Christ. A bishop who has to guard his flock is a fitting companion for today's readings.
study: Do my words build peace in my family and parish, or do I sometimes feed division with “smooth talk”?
If someone looked only at the fruit of my life this year, what kind of tree would they say I am?

lead: Today the calendar recalls the ancient stone cross of Mylapore, while the fast before Yaldo continues. The readings fit the day well. Paul, “the very least of all the saints”, is sent to bring the riches of Christ to the nations. In the Gospel Thomas, the apostle our tradition calls the apostle of India, asks the question that draws out one of the greatest sayings of Jesus. The riches of Christ reached this land, and the way to the Father is the way of the Cross.

r.h: The boundless riches of Christ
set: Paul writes as “a prisoner for Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles” (3:1). He has been explaining the “mystery” of God's plan: Gentiles are now fellow heirs and members of the same body (3:6). Today's verses describe his own role in that plan and what it means for the Church.
str: vv. 8–9: the smallest of the saints, the greatest of tasks.
v. 10: the Church makes God's wisdom known, even to heavenly powers.
vv. 11–12: all this in Christ, in whom we have access to God.
v. 13: do not lose heart because of my sufferings.
kw: Literally “leaster”, a comparative made from a superlative: less than the least. Paul has not forgotten that he once persecuted the Church (compare 1 Corinthians 15:9).

Literally “that cannot be tracked”, like a trail that goes on beyond the hunter's search. The same word appears in Romans 11:33. The POC's “ദുർഗ്രഹമായ” brings out that these riches are beyond our grasp.

“Many-coloured”, like a richly woven cloth, and the word occurs only here in the New Testament. The Churches of East and West, with their different rites and languages, are one small sign of this variety.
vv: this grace was given to me to bring to the Gentiles the news of the boundless riches of Christ,
Paul calls his mission a grace, not a burden or a career. The word “Gentiles” means us, the nations outside Israel, among them the peoples of India.
so that through the church the wisdom of God in its rich variety might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.

A surprising claim: the Church teaches the angels. When Jew and Gentile, rich and poor kneel together, heaven itself sees God's plan at work. St John Chrysostom draws the same conclusion in his homilies on this letter (in substance).
in whom we have access to God in boldness and confidence through faith in him.
Parrēsia, “boldness”, was the right of a citizen to speak openly. Through Christ the least of us may speak to God as a son or daughter speaks at home.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in the Church Christ fulfils and reveals his own mystery as the purpose of God's plan (CCC 772, which draws on this passage). This is why we can never treat the Church as a merely human organisation. She is the place where the plan hidden for ages can now be seen.

r.h: I am the way, and the truth, and the life
set: The setting is the Last Supper, on the night of the betrayal. Judas has gone out into the night (13:30), and Peter has just been told that he will deny Jesus three times (13:38). The disciples have heard that Jesus is going where they cannot follow (13:36). They are frightened and confused, and into this fear he speaks these words.
str: v. 1: do not be troubled; believe.
vv. 2–3: the promise of a place and of his return.
vv. 4–5: “you know the way”, and Thomas' honest objection.
v. 6: Jesus' answer.
kw: Stirred up, shaken. John uses the same verb of Jesus himself (11:33; 12:27; 13:21). He who is telling them not to be troubled has just been troubled in spirit himself. He knows what he is asking.
From the verb menein, to remain, one of John's favourite words. The stress is on a place to stay with the Father, not on the size or number of rooms.
Before they were called Christians, believers were known as people of “the Way” (Acts 9:2). Jesus does not only show a road; he is the road.
vv: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me.
Faith in Jesus is set beside faith in God: a quiet, staggering claim, made on the night he is to be arrested.
I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, there you may be also.
Heaven is described here not by its furniture but by a person: to be with him.
Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”

Thomas says little in John, and it is worth following. He is ready to die with Jesus (11:16), he asks this question, and he will make the highest confession in the Gospel: “My Lord and my God!” (20:28). The honest question leads to the great confession. Without Thomas' question we would not have the answer that follows.
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
Jesus gathers everything into three words: the road we walk, the truth we seek, and the life we were made for.
ch: The Catechism places this verse among the reasons for the Incarnation: the Word became flesh to be our model of holiness (CCC 459). St Augustine puts it memorably: as God, Christ is the homeland we are going to; as man, he is the way by which we go (in substance).

qa: If no one comes to the Father except through Jesus, what about the good people of other religions, here in India?

The Church holds both truths together. All salvation comes through Christ and his Church (CCC 846). Yet those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, but seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will, can attain salvation by the grace of Christ (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). So Christians speak of Jesus with confidence and of their neighbours with respect, and the duty of mission remains (CCC 848).
rite: The stone cross venerated at St Thomas Mount in Chennai was found in the sixteenth century. It carries a Pahlavi inscription, whose reading scholars have debated, and it belongs to a family of ancient crosses found in South India, among them those at Kottayam and Kadamattom. This much is History: Christians in India were carving the Cross here long before the Portuguese came. The account that the cross sweated on 18 December 1558 comes from Tradition. Tradition also places the martyrdom of St Thomas at Mylapore. The Malankara Church, with all the Thomas Christians, treasures this heritage; the Cross of our fathers still says what Jesus says today: this is the way.
study: Thomas was not afraid to say, “we do not know”. What honest question do I need to bring to Jesus today?
What do the old crosses of our land say to me about the faith I have received, and what am I handing on?

lead: Six days before Yaldo the readings ask two questions about the Coming One. Where will God dwell? Paul answers: in a people, Jews and Gentiles made one in Christ, built into a temple. Are you really the one? John the Baptist asks from prison, and Jesus answers by pointing to what is happening: the blind see, and the poor hear good news.

r.h: A dwelling place for God
set: Paul has reminded the Gentile believers that they were once “far off”, without hope and without God in the world (2:11–13). Now they have been brought near by the blood of Christ. Today's passage explains how. Its background is the deepest social division the first Christians knew: Jew and Gentile, separated by Law, custom and worship.
str: vv. 14–16: Christ is our peace: the wall down, one new humanity, reconciliation through the Cross.
vv. 17–18: peace proclaimed, and access to the Father.
vv. 19–22: the building: citizens, household, temple.
kw: An unusual word. It may recall the barrier in the Jerusalem Temple which kept Gentiles from the inner courts. Josephus describes it, and a stone warning from it, threatening death, was found in 1871. Paul himself was accused of bringing Greeks past it (Acts 21:28).
The right of approach into the presence of a king or to a sanctuary. It occurs again at 3:12.
The foundation stone that sets the line of the whole building (see Isaiah 28:16). The building has one Stone that holds it true.
vv: For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
Peace here is a person, not a treaty. “In his flesh” points to the Cross; it is also the flesh born at Bethlehem.
for through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father.
In one sentence, the whole Trinity and the pattern of all Christian prayer: through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. The great Anaphora of the Holy Qurbono follows this same movement.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
The two words described people without full rights. In God's house there are no second-class members.
in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.
The verb is present and ongoing. The temple is still under construction, and each of us is a living part of it.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this very passage when it speaks of the Jewish people: by his Cross Christ our Peace reconciled Jews and Gentiles, making both one in himself (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism names Christ as the cornerstone of the Church's building (CCC 756).

r.h: Go and tell John what you hear and see
set: V. 1 closes Jesus' instructions to the Twelve (chapter 10). John has been in prison since 4:12. According to Josephus, Herod Antipas held him in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. John had announced one who would come with an axe and fire (3:10–12). What he hears about Jesus sounds rather different.
str: v. 1: Jesus goes on teaching in the towns.
vv. 2–3: John's question.
vv. 4–5: Jesus' answer: a list of works that echo Isaiah.
v. 6: a beatitude.
kw: the one who is to come
A title of hope (see Psalm 118:26; Malachi 3:1) and John's own word: “one who is more powerful than I is coming after me” (3:11).
The same verb as John 16:1. To stumble on Jesus means to find him not what we had expected and to turn away.
vv: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?”
The question of this whole season, asked by its greatest preacher.
the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them.

Jesus does not say yes. He gives a list, woven from Isaiah (35:5–6; 61:1; see also 26:19), and lets John draw his own conclusion. Note where the list ends. After the dead are raised comes what seems small, yet is its climax: good news for the poor.
And blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.”
A beatitude for everyone who has had to give up their own picture of God's way of working.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' signs bear witness that the Father has sent him and invite belief in him, but that they can also be an occasion for “offence” (CCC 548, citing this verse). St John Chrysostom, in his homilies on Matthew, holds that John asked not for himself, but so that his own disciples might go and see (in substance).

qa: Did John the Baptist doubt?

The Fathers answered in different ways. Many, with St John Chrysostom, said that John asked for his disciples' sake. Others, and many modern commentators, think the question may be his own: a prisoner who had to wait for Jesus to fulfil God's plan differently than he expected. Either way, Jesus goes on at once to praise him highly (11:7–11). An honest question is not unbelief.
study: Whom do I still treat as a stranger or alien, in my parish, in my town? What would it mean for Christ's peace to break down that wall?
In what way has Jesus not been what I expected? Have I stumbled on it, or learned from it?

lead: This is the Sixth Sunday of Suboro, the last before Yaldo, and the Church spends it among names and family trees. The Evening Gospel (Matthew 1:1–17) gives the genealogy of Jesus, from Abraham through David and through the exile to “Joseph the husband of Mary”. The Old Testament list of Jacob's household going down to Egypt (Genesis 46:8–27) has Judah, Perez and Hezron in it, the same names that stand at the head of Matthew's line. These lists are not dull. They say that God's salvation enters real history through real families, some faithful and some not.

The other readings follow the promise along that line. God promises Solomon a throne, and warns that the house can be lost (1 Kings 9:3–7). The prophets looked beyond that loss: Isaiah saw a shoot from the stump (Isaiah 11:1–9), and Jeremiah, as the kingdom was collapsing, announced “a righteous Branch” for David (Jeremiah 23:5–8). In Acts (3:20–26) Peter returns to the oldest word of all, spoken to Abraham: “in your descendants all the families of the earth shall be blessed”.

We study three readings closely: Isaiah 11:1–9, the Old Testament lesson closest to the Gospel; Hebrews 7:14–17, the Pauline reading, which says what a family tree could not give Jesus; and Luke 2:1–5, where the promise walks down a road toward Bethlehem. The key words are root, descent and registered.

r.h: A shoot from the stump of Jesse
set: Isaiah preached in Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, when Assyria was swallowing up the nations around Judah and the kings of David's line were often a disappointment. The chapter before ends with a terrible image: the Lord “will hack down the thickets of the forest with an ax” (10:34). Then comes today's first verse, in the same landscape of felled trees.

Notice that the prophet says Jesse, not David. Going behind the king to his father, a farmer of Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:1), suggests that God will begin again from the beginning, from small and humble things.
str: vv. 1–3a: the shoot and the Spirit who rests on him.
vv. 3b–5: his justice, especially for the poor.
vv. 6–8: creation at peace: predators and their prey, a child among snakes.
v. 9: no more harm on God's holy mountain; the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord.
kw: What is left after the tree is cut. It looks dead. Isaiah had already spoken of a holy seed in a stump (6:13).
A green shoot. Many scholars see a play on this word behind Matthew 2:23, where Jesus of Nazareth “will be called a Nazorean”. Jeremiah 23:5 uses another Hebrew word (ṣemaḥ) for the same hope.

The Spirit who came on Israel's judges and on David (1 Samuel 16:13). Here the Spirit rests on the king and stays. The Hebrew names six qualities in three pairs. The Greek and Latin Bibles render “fear of the Lord” in two different ways (piety and fear), and from this the Church's tradition counts the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.
In Hebrew “knowing” means more than having information. It is a relationship of faithful love. For Isaiah that knowledge will one day cover the earth.
vv: A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots.

Hope in Isaiah starts where everything seems finished. St Ambrose and St Jerome read the “shoot” (Latin virga) as the Virgin Mary (virgo), and the flower that rises from it as Christ (in substance). The word play exists only in Latin, but the thought has fed Christian prayer ever since.
The spirit of the Lord shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord.
In the Gospels the Spirit descends and rests on Jesus at his baptism (Luke 3:22), and he applies Isaiah's promise of the anointed one to himself in Nazareth (Luke 4:18, from Isaiah 61).
but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth;
The first act of this king is to do justice for those who have no one else. “The rod of his mouth” in the same verse means that he rules by his word. He needs no army.
The wolf shall live with the lamb, the leopard shall lie down with the kid,
Eden's peace comes back, and the enmity between serpent and human is also healed (v. 8). See the Questions below.
and a little child shall lead them.
Isaiah probably means only that the world will be so safe that a child can herd these animals. Christians, reading it five days before Yaldo, can hardly fail to think of another Child.
for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea.
This is the reason why the animals are at peace. Harm ends when people truly know God. Habakkuk 2:14 repeats this promise.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses to describe the Spirit who rests on the Messiah (CCC 712; see also 1286) and lists the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord (CCC 1831). What was promised to the shoot of Jesse is shared with his members in Baptism and in Holy Mooron, the chrism of our Syriac tradition. The last book of the Bible gives the risen Lord this title: “I am the root and the descendant of David” (Revelation 22:16). He is the shoot from David's line, and he is also the root from which David came.

r.h: A priest by the power of an indestructible life
set: The lectionary reads Hebrews with the Pauline epistles, as the Church has long received it among the letters linked with St Paul, though the letter does not name its author. Chapter 7 builds an argument on one verse, Psalm 110:4, and on the mysterious figure of Melchizedek, who brought out bread and wine to Abraham (Genesis 14:18).

Under the Law, priesthood came by descent from Levi and Aaron. So there is a problem, which the writer states openly: Jesus was of the wrong tribe. Today's genealogies prove that Jesus is a son of Judah and David; they cannot make him a priest.
str: v. 14: the fact: our Lord came from Judah, not Levi.
v. 15: therefore a different kind of priest has arisen.
v. 16: the basis of his priesthood: not descent, but life.
v. 17: the proof from Scripture (Psalm 110:4).
kw: The verb anatellō is used of a shoot sprouting or of the sun rising. The Greek Old Testament uses the related noun anatolē for the “Branch” of Jeremiah 23:5, one of today's readings. So the writer's word for Jesus' descent may carry a hint of that promise.
Not a religious order as we use the word, but a rank or kind. Jesus' priesthood is of Melchizedek's kind, without a family list.
“That cannot be dissolved”. Levitical priests died and had to be replaced (7:23). Jesus' priesthood rests on a life that death has not been able to break.
vv: For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah,
This is one of the few places outside the Gospels where the New Testament refers to Jesus' earthly family line. Everybody, it seems, knew it.
one who has become a priest, not through a legal requirement concerning physical descent, but through the power of an indestructible life.

The Greek speaks of a “fleshly” requirement, contrasted with “life”. Here is the key to the two kinds of lists. A family tree can pass on a name and a throne. It cannot pass on what Jesus offers. His priesthood rests on who he is, risen and alive for ever.
“You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”
The word “forever” is what the writer wants us to hear. Only someone who lives forever can be a priest forever.
ch: The Catechism says that Christian tradition sees Melchizedek as a figure of the priesthood of Christ, the unique “high priest after the order of Melchizedek”, and that all the priesthood of the Old Covenant finds its fulfilment in him (CCC 1544). His sacrifice is made present in the Eucharist, and his priesthood is shared by those who serve at the altar (CCC 1545). St Cyprian already saw Melchizedek's bread and wine as a figure of the Lord's sacrifice (Letter 63, in substance). Whenever a priest of the Malankara Church stands at the altar, he acts in the priesthood of the Son of Judah.

r.h: Joseph and Mary go up to Bethlehem
set: Luke sets the birth of Jesus on the stage of world history. Augustus ruled from 27 BC to AD 14 and was praised for bringing peace to the Mediterranean world. An inscription from Priene in Asia Minor (9 BC) calls his birthday the beginning of good news (euangelia) for the world, and honours him as a saviour. A few verses later the angel will use the same language for a baby in a manger: “good news”, “a Savior” (2:10–11).

Luke draws a sharp contrast: the man in Rome issues a decree, and the true King travels as one of those who must obey it. Nazareth and Bethlehem are several days' walk apart, and the road to the hill country goes up.
str: vv. 1–2: the imperial decree.
v. 3: everyone goes to be registered.
vv. 4–5: Joseph and Mary, from Nazareth to the city of David.
kw: To be entered on a list, as for tax. On the Sunday of family lists, here is yet another list. The Son of God allows his name to be written down on Caesar's roll.
Joseph's descent is what sends him to Bethlehem. The angel has already called Jesus heir to “the throne of his ancestor David” (1:32), and that claim comes through Joseph, the legal father.

The NRSV “engaged” follows the Greek. Some ancient versions and many later manuscripts read “wife”, in one form or another, and the Malayalam POC gives “ഭാര്യ”. Matthew tells us that Joseph had by then taken her into his home (Matthew 1:24).
The word occurs only here in the New Testament. Luke's language is plain and his tone quiet, even at this great moment.
vv: In those days a decree went out from Emperor Augustus that all the world should be registered.

“All the world” is the Roman way of speaking of the empire. The most powerful man alive signs a paper, and without knowing it he moves one family to the place of the prophecy. God's plan makes use of even Caesar's paperwork.
This was the first registration and was taken while Quirinius was governor of Syria.
On the historical question see the Questions below.
Joseph also went from the town of Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, because he was descended from the house and family of David.

In the Old Testament “the city of David” normally means Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:7). Luke gives the title to the humble village where David was a shepherd. Here he passes over the royal capital. Micah had said: “But you, O Bethlehem of Ephrathah, who are one of the little clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to rule in Israel” (Micah 5:2).
He went to be registered with Mary, to whom he was engaged and who was expecting a child.
No word of complaint is recorded. Joseph and Mary obey an unwelcome order, and by doing so they obey God without seeing how. This verse is a picture of ordinary faith in hard times.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus was born at Bethlehem at the time of King Herod the Great and the emperor Caesar Augustus (CCC 423), which keeps the faith rooted in real history, and that he was born in humble surroundings, into a poor family (CCC 525). St Gregory the Great, preaching at Christmas, asks why the world was being registered when the Lord was about to be born, and answers: because he was appearing in the flesh who would register his chosen ones in eternity (in substance). He also notes the name Bethlehem, “house of bread”: the Bread of heaven was born there (in substance). The Hebrew is bêt leḥem. The bread of Bethlehem comes to us on the altar in every Holy Qurbono.

qa: Why do Matthew and Luke give different genealogies? And why trace Jesus through Joseph if Joseph was not his natural father?

Matthew (1:1–17) goes down from Abraham through Solomon; Luke (3:23–38) goes up from Jesus through David's son Nathan all the way to Adam, and they name different fathers for Joseph (Jacob in Matthew 1:16; Heli in Luke 3:23). Early Christians already noticed this. Julius Africanus, for example, proposed an explanation from the Jewish law of levirate marriage. No solution is certain, and it is best to admit this. What matters is that each list has its own purpose: Matthew arranges his in three groups of fourteen, the numerical value of David's name in Hebrew, to show a Son of David; Luke shows a Son of Adam for all humanity. Both evangelists are careful about Joseph. Matthew breaks his own pattern at 1:16, “Mary, of whom Jesus was born”, and Luke writes “as was thought” (3:23). By naming and accepting the child, Joseph, “son of David” (Matthew 1:20), gives him a legal place in David's line (see CCC 437).
Is Luke wrong about the census of Quirinius?

This is a real historical difficulty. Luke himself places the birth of Jesus in the days of Herod the Great (1:5), who died in 4 BC, whereas Josephus records a census under Quirinius as governor of Syria around AD 6. Proposals have been made: an earlier enrolment, an earlier post held by Quirinius, or a reading of the Greek as “before” Quirinius was governor. None has convinced everyone, and evidence is lacking. A Catholic reader need not hide the problem or fear it. Luke's teaching is clear: the birth of Jesus took place under Roman rule, in real time, and God was at work through it.
Will the wolf really live with the lamb?

Isaiah is writing poetry, and Christians have read these verses in more than one way. Some, like St Irenaeus, expected a renewed creation in a literal sense; others have seen in the animals a picture of hostile peoples reconciled in the Church. Both have something true. Already where Christ reigns, enemies sit at one table. And the Church also hopes for a new heaven and a new earth, in which creation itself shares in redemption (Romans 8:21; CCC 1042–1047).
rite: Yaldo is the Syriac word for birth. On this Sixth Sunday of Suboro, the last before Yaldo, the Malankara Church completes the journey of its Annunciation Sundays: from the message to Zechariah to the road to Bethlehem. The Twenty-Five Days' Fast is near its end, and Yaldo falls this year on Friday 25 December. A good way to keep these last days is to read aloud at home the names of Matthew 1, to pray for our own families and ancestors, some of whom were saints and some not, and to prepare for confession. The God who wrote Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah into his Son's family tree (Matthew 1:3, 5, 6) can write our family into his plan as well.
study: Isaiah sees life in a stump that looks dead. Where in my family or parish do I need to look for a green shoot?
The list of the Spirit's gifts in Isaiah 11:2 is given to us in Baptism. Which of them do I most need to ask for this week?
Joseph and Mary obeyed an unwelcome government order, and God used it. What inconvenient duty in my life may be part of God's plan?
Which names in my family tree would I like to give thanks for, and which would I like to pray for, before Yaldo?

lead: Four days before Yaldo, at the time of the longest nights in the northern half of the world, the Church reads the opening of John: “The light shines in the darkness.” With it comes Paul's greeting to the Christians of Rome, full of thanks and longing. The Word who was with God from the beginning is the same One whose good news drives Paul across the world, a debt he says he owes to every people.

r.h: Your faith is proclaimed throughout the world
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57 (see 16:1, 23). He had neither founded nor yet visited this Church. He was planning to go on to Spain and to visit Rome on the way (15:23–24). The opening of the letter is therefore a careful, courteous introduction, by an apostle to a community that does not know him personally.
str: v. 8: thanksgiving for their faith.
vv. 9–10: his constant prayer, and his wish to come.
vv. 11–12: why he wants to come: to give, and to receive.
vv. 13–15: his plan, and his debt to all people.
kw: The same family of words as “Eucharist”. Paul's letters regularly begin with thanksgiving for what God is already doing in others.
The word for sacred service. Paul serves God “with my spirit”, and his preaching of the Gospel is itself his worship (see 15:16).
A striking word: Paul owes the Gospel to everyone. It was entrusted to him for them, so he must deliver it.
vv: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the world.
“Through Jesus Christ”: even thanks goes through the Mediator. The faith of an ordinary community in the capital was news in the whole Christian world.
or rather so that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine.
A lovely correction. The great apostle begins to say that he will strengthen them, and then adds that he too needs them. Every real pastoral visit runs in both directions.
I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish
“Barbarians” is the Greeks' word for those who did not speak Greek. Paul crosses the great divides of his culture: language, and education. The Gospel is not for the refined alone.
ch: St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom in the early second century, wrote to the same Church of Rome, praising it as presiding in love, words the Catechism recalls when it speaks of Rome and the communion of the Churches (CCC 834). So the see of Antioch, our own West Syriac heritage, speaks to Rome of faith and love. On intercession among Christians as a mark of the first communities, see CCC 2636.

r.h: In him was life, and the life was light
set: Matthew opens with a genealogy and Luke with a census. John begins before there was any census, before time. His first words are the first words of the Greek Bible: “In the beginning” (Genesis 1:1). Then comes the surprise. Genesis goes on, “God created”; John goes on, “was the Word”. This Prologue (1:1–18) is the great hymn of the Incarnation, and it reaches its summit at 1:14.
str: vv. 1–2: the Word and God, before all things.
v. 3: all things through him.
vv. 4–5: life and light; the darkness does not overcome.
kw: A rich term. For John's Jewish readers it recalled the creating word of God (“God said”, Genesis 1:3) and Wisdom, who was beside God at creation (Proverbs 8:22–31). For Greek readers it also carried the sense of reason and order in the world. John gathers all this into one person.
Pros here can carry a sense of movement toward. The Word is not merely beside God, but turned toward him, in living relation.
The Greek verb can mean to overcome and also to grasp or understand. John may intend both: the darkness neither understood nor defeated the light.
vv: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

Three short statements. The Word existed before all creation; the Word is distinct from the Father; the Word is truly God. In the last phrase the Greek has no article before “God” (theos ēn ho logos). This does not mean “a god”. Placed first for emphasis, the word says what the Word is, without making him identical with the Person of the Father.
All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.
John's verbs are careful. The Word “was”; things “came into being”. All that begins, begins through him. So he himself does not belong among the created things, as Arius would later claim.
What has come into being in him was life, and the life was the light of all people.

A note on the text. The oldest Greek manuscripts have little or no punctuation, and the words “What has come into being” can be joined either to v. 4, as the NRSV does with many early Fathers, or to v. 3, as many later Fathers do and as the Malayalam POC does (“… അവനിൽ ജീവനുണ്ടായിരുന്നു”). The faith is the same in both: life is found in the Word.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.
“Shines” is present; “did not overcome” is past. The battle has an outcome already, and the light is still shining. This is the verse to carry through the longest nights.
ch: The Council of Nicaea (325) confessed against Arius that the Son is “consubstantial” with the Father (CCC 242), and the Creed sings “Light from Light”. The Catechism quotes these verses on creation through the Word (CCC 291). St Augustine says in his Confessions (VII.9) that he found something of “In the beginning was the Word” among the philosophers, but not that “the Word became flesh” (in substance). In four days the Church will celebrate that very thing.

study: To whom do I owe the Gospel, as Paul says he does? Who around me has never heard it from someone they trust?
Where in my life does the darkness seem strongest? What would it mean to believe today that it did not, and will not, overcome the light?

lead: Three days before Yaldo, both readings ask who has found whom. Paul reminds the Galatians that their faith began when they were known by God, and he cannot understand why they would go back to slavery. John's prologue shows a man sent from God, a witness who is not the light himself, pointing to the true light that is already on its way into the world. God takes the first step in both readings: he knows us before we know him, and he sends before anyone asks.

r.h: Known by God
set: Paul founded the churches of Galatia, in the centre of Asia Minor, among Gentiles. After he left, other teachers urged these believers to be circumcised and to keep the Law of Moses as the way to belong fully to God's people. Paul has just told them that they are children and heirs through Christ (4:4–7). Now he turns from teaching to pleading. For him, going back under the Law as if Christ were not enough would be like returning to the slavery they knew before they believed.
str: v. 8: what they once were: slaves of gods that are no gods.
v. 9: what they are now: known by God. Then the astonished question: why go back?
v. 10: the evidence: anxious keeping of days and seasons.
v. 11: Paul's fear that his work has been wasted.
kw: Paul corrects himself in mid sentence: you have come to know God, “or rather to be known by God”. In the Bible, to be known by God means to be chosen and loved by him, not merely noticed. The first move in the relationship is always God's.

The word means basic elements, the first letters of an alphabet or the elements of the world. Scholars still discuss its exact sense here: the powers that people believed ruled the world and the stars, or the elementary rules of religious life before Christ. Paul's two adjectives say what he thinks of them: “weak and beggarly”.
A verb of close, watchful attention, as one might anxiously watch a calendar. Paul's worry is the spirit of this watching: as if a person could secure God's favour by getting the dates right.
vv: Now, however, that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elemental spirits?

Paul's bold move is to put two things side by side: the pagan past of the Galatians and the Law-keeping they are now being offered. He is not calling the Law of Moses pagan (see Romans 7:12). He means that anything held on to as a rival to Christ leaves a person enslaved.
You are observing special days, and months, and seasons, and years.
Most likely the sabbaths, new moons, festivals and sabbatical years of the Jewish calendar, urged on these Gentiles as necessary for salvation. Compare Colossians 2:16–17.
I am afraid that my work for you may have been wasted.
This is the voice of a pastor rather than a judge. A few verses later he calls them “my little children” and speaks of being in the pain of childbirth for them (4:19).
ch: The Church hears in this passage the priority of grace. The Catechism teaches that the preparation of man for the reception of grace is already a work of grace (CCC 2001), and St John says the same in other words: “In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us” (1 John 4:10). Paul's warning is not against the Church's feasts but against any religion that tries to earn what God has already given in his Son.

r.h: The true light was coming
set: The prologue of John (1:1–18) has the lofty rhythm of a hymn, and into it the evangelist twice brings a plain historical figure: John (vv. 6–8 and v. 15). The Fourth Gospel never calls him “the Baptist”; he is simply John, and his whole task is to testify. After the eternal Word of vv. 1–5 comes a man with a name, sent at a moment in history. The Malankara faithful kept his birth earlier in Suboro; today he stands at the door of the feast.
str: v. 6: a man sent from God, named John.
v. 7: his mission: to testify, so that all might believe.
v. 8: what he is not: he is not the light.
v. 9: the true light is on its way into the world.
kw: From the verb that gives us the word “apostle”. John does not come on his own account. His authority lies entirely in the One who sends him.

A favourite word of this Gospel, and a word from the courtroom. A witness speaks of what he has seen and does not draw attention to himself. The later Christian word “martyr” grows from the same root.
Not simply true as opposed to false, but the real thing as against its shadows. Other lights have been given to the world; this is the light from which they all come.
vv: He came as a witness to testify to the light, so that all might believe through him.
“All”: from the first page the Gospel has the whole world in view. John's work is finished when people believe, and they believe in Christ, not in John (see 3:30).
He himself was not the light, but he came to testify to the light.
Every preacher, catechist and parent should know this verse. Those who bring others to Christ are not the light, and they do not need to be.
The true light, which enlightens everyone, was coming into the world.

A note on the text. The Greek can be read in two ways: the light was “coming into the world” (the NRSV, the POC), or the light enlightens “everyone coming into the world” (the Latin Vulgate). Either way the light is meant for every human being.
ch: The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate forerunner, sent to prepare his way (CCC 523). St Augustine contrasts John, the voice, with Christ, the Word: the voice sounds and passes, and the Word remains (in substance, Sermon 293). The Church also takes up v. 9 when she speaks of Baptism as enlightenment, in which the believer receives the Word, “the true light”, and becomes a child of light (CCC 1216). The Second Vatican Council sees whatever is good and true among those who do not yet know the Gospel as given by him who enlightens all people (Lumen Gentium 16).

qa: If Paul scolds people for keeping days and seasons, why do we keep Yaldo?

Paul is speaking against the idea that keeping a calendar makes us right with God, and against imposing that on Gentile believers as necessary for salvation. The Church's year does something different. It does not earn anything from God. It unfolds the mystery of Christ through the year, so that we can enter into what he has already done for us (Sacrosanctum Concilium 102; CCC 1163). We keep Yaldo because God has known us first, and we rejoice in that.
study: Paul says it is more important to be known by God than to know God. How does that change the way I pray?
John the witness was “not the light”. Whom has God used as a witness for me, and for whom could I do the same this Christmas?

lead: Today's readings speak of what God gives to those who receive him. Paul tells the Colossians that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ, so they need not look elsewhere. John says that the Word came to his own, and that those who received him were given power to become children of God. The riches of Christmas are not a thing but a Person, and the way into them is to receive him.

r.h: All the treasures in Christ
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had not founded this church; it came to faith through Epaphras (1:7), and Paul writes as a prisoner (4:18) to people who had never met him. Some teaching was circulating among them that offered a deeper wisdom, with special rules and visions (2:8, 16–18). The Church has received the letter under Paul's name, though many scholars think a close disciple may have had a hand in it.
str: v. 1: Paul's struggle for people he has never seen.
vv. 2–3: his aim: hearts encouraged and united, and knowledge of God's mystery, Christ.
v. 4: why he says this: so that no one will deceive them.
v. 5: absent in body, present in spirit.
kw: For Paul this is not a puzzle or a secret for the initiated. It is God's plan, once hidden and now opened to all, and he says what it is: Christ himself.
The treasures are hidden in Christ, but not hidden from believers. Paul may be answering people who offered secret knowledge: there is no treasure outside of him that one would need to look for.
A word found only here in the New Testament: speech that persuades by sounding convincing rather than by being true.
vv: I want their hearts to be encouraged and united in love, so that they may have all the riches of assured understanding and have the knowledge of God’s mystery, that is, Christ himself,

A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts differ a good deal in this phrase. The reading that the NRSV and POC follow, found in the very old papyrus P46 and in Codex Vaticanus, identifies the mystery with Christ. Note also the order: love comes first, and understanding grows in a community united in love.
