in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
This is the centre of the passage. Jewish wisdom writings speak of wisdom as a treasure to be sought (Proverbs 2:1–5). Paul says where it is to be found.
For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, and I rejoice to see your morale and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
The Greek words behind “morale” (taxis) and “firmness” (stereōma) can both be used of soldiers in good order holding a line. The community is standing firm, and Paul is glad of it.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the deepest truth about God and about human salvation shines out in Christ, who is both the mediator and the fullness of all revelation (Dei Verbum 2). St John of the Cross, writing on this verse in his Spiritual Canticle, says that however much the saints have discovered in Christ, most of it remains still to be said: he is like a rich mine with many pockets of treasure, and however deep one digs, one never reaches the end (in substance).

r.h: Power to become children of God
set: The prologue moves from the true light (v. 9) to the response it receives. Two refusals come first, by the world and by “his own”, and then the great exception: those who received him. These verses already contain, in small, the plot of the entire Gospel: chapters 1–12 tell of the light offered and refused, and chapters 13–21 are for those who receive him.
str: v. 10: the world, made through him, did not know him.
v. 11: his own people did not accept him.
v. 12: those who received him are given power to become God's children.
v. 13: this birth comes from God.
kw: In John this can mean the good creation God loves (3:16), or humanity as it closes itself against him (here, in the last clause). The world's maker came to it, and it did not recognize him.
The first phrase is neuter, “what was his own”, and could almost be translated “he came home”. The second is masculine: the people of his house.
This is not physical strength but a right or authority that is given. Being a child of God is not something we have by nature or claim for ourselves. It is a gift, and to receive it is to believe.
vv: He came to what was his own, and his own people did not accept him.

This verse must not be used to blame the Jewish people. Many of “his own” did receive him: Mary, Joseph, John, the apostles and the first Church were all Jews. The Church teaches that the Jews are not to be held collectively responsible for the rejection of Jesus (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The verse is a warning for every Christian who has known Christ for a long time, since it is possible to be close to him and not receive him.
But to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave power to become children of God,

“All” opens the door: no race, family or merit is required. Receiving and believing explain each other. The tense in “received” points to the moment of acceptance, and “believed” (a present participle in Greek) to an ongoing life of faith.
who were born, not of blood or of the will of the flesh or of the will of man, but of God.

A note on the text. All Greek manuscripts have the plural, “who were born”, speaking of believers. A few early Latin witnesses and some early writers, among them Irenaeus and Tertullian, read the singular, “who was born”, referring to Christ's birth from the Virgin. Most Bibles follow the plural, but the link between the two births is real: he was born of God so that we might be.
ch: The Catechism names this among the reasons for the Incarnation: the Word became flesh to make us “partakers of the divine nature” (CCC 460, quoting 2 Peter 1:4). It quotes St Irenaeus, who says the Word became man so that man might become a son of God, and St Athanasius, who says the Son of God became man so that we might become God. Baptism is the rebirth that John means here (see John 3:5; CCC 1213).

study: Where do I go looking for wisdom or security apart from Christ? What would it mean to believe that the treasure is already in him?
How can I, who have long known Christ, still fail to receive him when he comes to what is his own, my home, my family, my day?

lead: On the eve of Yaldo the Church reads two passages about seeing God. Paul says that God's power has been visible in creation from the beginning, yet human beings exchanged his glory for images of mortal things. John answers with the words the whole season has been waiting for: “And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory”. People made images of God that could not save them; now God himself gives us the true Image, in a child.

r.h: They exchanged the glory
set: Paul writes to the Christians of Rome, a church he had not yet visited, probably from Corinth around AD 57. He has just announced his theme: the gospel is “the power of God for salvation to everyone who has faith” (1:16). Before explaining the remedy, he describes the sickness. In 1:18–32 he looks at the Gentile world, and in chapter 2 he turns to those who have the Law, in order to conclude that all have sinned and all need Christ (3:22–23). His language echoes the Book of Wisdom on people who could have known the Creator from his works (Wisdom 13:1–9).
str: v. 18: God's wrath against the suppression of truth.
vv. 19–20: what can be known of God is plain from creation, so they are without excuse.
v. 21: they knew God, but neither honoured nor thanked him.
vv. 22–23: the great exchange: glory for images.
kw: Not a burst of bad temper, but God's settled opposition to what destroys his creatures. In the verses following this reading it takes a sobering form: God lets people have what they have chosen (1:24, 26, 28).
A word found only here in the New Testament. It means what makes God to be God, as far as it can be perceived through his works.
The verb recalls Psalm 106:20, where Israel at Horeb “exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox”. Paul uses Israel's own confession to describe the sin of all humanity.
vv: Ever since the creation of the world his eternal power and divine nature, invisible though they are, have been understood and seen through the things he has made.

This is the great biblical text on what the human mind can know of God from creation. It does not mean that everyone has an easy or complete knowledge of God, only that creation really does speak of him.
for though they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their senseless minds were darkened.

Notice where it begins: with a failure to give thanks. For Paul, ingratitude is the root. Christians call their chief act of worship Eucharist, thanksgiving, and the Holy Qurbono is the opposite of this verse.
and they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling a mortal human being or birds or four-footed animals or reptiles.
The list goes downward, from man to reptile. People become like what they worship. Tonight the order is turned upside down: the glory of the immortal God takes a mortal human body.
ch: The First Vatican Council taught, on the basis of this passage, that God can be known with certainty from created things by the natural light of human reason (Dei Filius, ch. 2; CCC 36). The Catechism adds that in our present condition we need God's revelation to know these truths easily and without error (CCC 37–38). St John of Damascus draws the line that leads to tonight: before, God who has no body could not be pictured; now that he has made himself visible in the flesh, I can make an image of what I have seen of God (in substance; CCC 1159). The image Paul condemns is one that replaces God; the image the Church honours points to the God who took a face.

r.h: The Word became flesh
set: These verses are the summit of the prologue. Until now the Word has been spoken of in terms of creation and light. Now comes the sentence on which all Christian faith turns. Behind it stands the story of Exodus: God's glory filling the tent in the desert (Exodus 40:34), and Moses asking to see that glory and being told that no one can see God's face (Exodus 33:18–20). John has this story in mind when he names Moses in v. 17 and says in v. 18 that no one has ever seen God.
str: v. 14: the Word becomes flesh and dwells among us; we have seen his glory.
v. 15: John's testimony: the one coming after him was before him.
v. 16: from his fullness, grace upon grace.
v. 17: Moses and Jesus Christ. This is the first time the Prologue uses the name of Jesus.
v. 18: the only Son has made the unseen God known.
kw: A surprising word. John does not say that the Word became “a man” in a general way, but “flesh”, human nature in its weakness and mortality. This word excludes any idea that the Son only seemed to be human.
From skēnē, “tent”, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the tabernacle. The place where God meets his people is now the body of a child.
Literally “grace in place of grace”. It is an image of gift following gift. It may also mean that the grace of Christ succeeds the grace given through Moses, as v. 17 goes on to suggest.

From the verb that gives us the word “exegesis”. It means to lead out, to explain, to tell the whole story. The Son is the living exegesis of the Father: if we want to know what God is like, we read Jesus.
vv: And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father’s only son, full of grace and truth.

“Full of grace and truth” probably echoes the words God proclaims of himself to Moses, “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). The God who showed Moses his back now shows his glory in a human face. “We have seen”: the Gospel speaks here as an eyewitness community.
The law indeed was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
John does not set Moses against Jesus as bad against good: the Law was God's gift. There is no “but” in the Greek. The verse shows the gift and its fullness side by side.
No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known.

A note on the text. Some of the oldest Greek manuscripts (P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) read “God the only Son”, which the NRSV and POC follow. Many others, and the Latin Vulgate, read “the only Son”. The prologue ends as it began, with the Word who is God (1:1). The phrase “close to the Father’s heart” is literally “in the bosom of the Father”, the place of closest love. Compare the beloved disciple at the Supper (13:23).
ch: From v. 14 the Church takes the word Incarnation (CCC 461). The great Councils guard this verse: the Word truly became flesh, one Person, true God and true man (CCC 464–469). In faithfulness to the same mystery, the Syriac Fathers sing of it in wonder. St Ephrem in his Hymns on the Nativity marvels that the Lord of all lies in the arms of Mary, the Ancient of Days a little child (in substance). The Catholic Church and the Syriac Orthodox Church, with which the Malankara tradition shares its roots, have together confessed one Christ, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity (common declarations of Pope Paul VI and Pope John Paul II with Syriac Orthodox Patriarchs, 1971 and 1984).

qa: Paul says people are “without excuse”. Does this mean that those who never heard of Christ are lost?

Paul is making an argument about sin, not giving a verdict on each person's soul. He wants to show that everyone needs Christ. The Church teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, yet seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will as their conscience shows it, can attain salvation, moved by grace (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). Christians are still sent to proclaim Christ to all (CCC 848–851), because he is the light they are seeking.
study: What have I been putting in the place of God: success, approval, money, security? What would giving thanks do to that?
“The Word became flesh.” Tonight, what does it change for me that God has a human face and body?

lead: Yaldo, the Syriac word for birth, gathers all the promises of Suboro into one night and day. The Evening Gospel gives the mystery in its deepest form: “And the Word became flesh and lived among us” (John 1:14). The Old Testament lessons then recall how God has worked through births before this one: Isaac, born to old Sarah, who says, “God has brought laughter for me” (Genesis 21:6); a son promised to the childless Shunammite woman (2 Kings 4:8–17); the ruler to come from little Bethlehem (Micah 5:1–4); and Isaiah's song, “For a child has been born for us, a son given to us” (Isaiah 9:6). In the Acts of the Apostles Peter declares that all the prophets “predicted these days” and that God sent his servant first “to bless you” (Acts 3:24, 26).

The three readings studied here form one line. Micah names the place: not the capital but a small village, from which a shepherd will come. Hebrews names the office: this child of the tribe of Judah is a priest for ever. Matthew shows who comes to him: wise men from the East, while those nearby are troubled. Place, priest and nations: a small town, an endless life, and a whole world on its knees.

r.h: From you, little Bethlehem
set: Micah came from Moresheth, a small town in the Judean lowlands, and prophesied in the late eighth century BC, in the time of Isaiah (Micah 1:1). He saw Assyria destroy the northern kingdom, and he saw Judah invaded and Jerusalem under pressure. He speaks sharply against the wealthy and powerful of the capital, who oppress the poor (2:1–2; 3:1–3).

This oracle begins in that crisis. The city is besieged, and its ruler is humiliated. Then the prophet looks away from the capital altogether, back to the village where David's family began. God's new beginning will come from where the old one started. A note on numbering: the Hebrew Bible counts this chapter one verse differently, so the Bethlehem verse is 5:1 in Hebrew and 5:2 in the NRSV and POC.
str: v. 1: Jerusalem under siege; its ruler struck on the cheek.
v. 2: the promise to Bethlehem Ephrathah.
v. 3: God gives his people up until “she who is in labor” has given birth, and then the scattered return.
v. 4: the coming ruler shepherds the flock in the strength of the Lord, and his greatness reaches the ends of the earth.
¶ The contrast is the point. Above stands a ruler with no power, struck in the face. Below is a small clan and a woman in labour, and from them comes a shepherd whose greatness has no limits.
kw: The clan name of David's family and the district around Bethlehem (Ruth 1:2; 1 Samuel 17:12). By using the old family name, Micah takes us back before the palace and before Jerusalem, to Jesse's sons and the sheep.

The word means small or young, and it is the word used for the youngest. David himself was the youngest son, called in from the flock (1 Samuel 16:11–13). God has a habit of choosing what is small (Deuteronomy 7:7).

Literally “his goings out”. “From of old, from ancient days” may first of all have meant the ancient line of David. Reading this verse in the light of Christ, the Church has heard in it more than the prophet could have spelled out: the Son's eternal birth from the Father.
The word for what David did before he was king, and the word by which God himself is described (Psalm 23:1). True rule, for the Bible, is feeding the flock.
vv: But you, O Bethlehem of Ephrathah, who are one of the little clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to rule in Israel, whose origin is from of old, from ancient days.

“For me”: this ruler comes for God's purposes and not for his own. The name Bethlehem (bêt leḥem) means “house of bread”, and the Fathers loved to note that the One who is the Bread of Life was born there and laid in a feeding trough.
Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labor has brought forth; then the rest of his kindred shall return to the people of Israel.

The woman is not named. The picture recalls Daughter Zion in labour (4:9–10) and the young woman of Isaiah 7:14, since Isaiah was Micah's contemporary. The Church reads her as Mary. The Second Vatican Council's teaching on Mary points to this very passage alongside Isaiah 7:14 (Lumen Gentium 55).
And he shall stand and feed his flock in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God.
He stands, while the ruler of v. 1 is struck down. His strength is not his own: it is “in the strength of the Lord”. The following verse in the NRSV adds, “and he shall be the one of peace”.
ch: Matthew has the chief priests and scribes quote this verse to Herod (Matthew 2:6). The evangelist's version differs from Micah: he says “by no means least”, where Micah says “little”, and he joins it to God's word to David, “It is you who shall be shepherd of my people Israel” (2 Samuel 5:2). Christ has changed Bethlehem's rank.

St Justin Martyr in the second century cites Micah in his dialogue with Trypho and speaks of the birth in a cave near the village (Dialogue with Trypho 78). Origen also cites Micah and says that the cave and the manger were still shown at Bethlehem in his day (Against Celsus 1.51). The Catechism sees in this hidden birth the mystery of the kingdom: to enter it, one must become small (CCC 525–526).

r.h: A priest for ever
set: Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). It is a sermon to Christians who are growing tired, and in chapters 7–10 it presents Christ as high priest. Its author is not named; the Church has received it among the letters linked with St Paul.

The author has an obvious problem. In the Law of Moses, priests came only from the tribe of Levi, and Jesus was of the tribe of Judah. His answer draws on two passages. In Genesis 14:18–20 Melchizedek, king of Salem and “priest of God Most High”, appears without any family record, brings out bread and wine, and blesses Abraham. In Psalm 110:4 God swears an oath to the Messiah-king: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”. So Scripture itself had promised a priesthood not based on descent from Levi. It is fitting to hear this on the day we keep the birth of a child of Judah.
str: v. 14: the fact: the Lord descended from Judah, and Moses said nothing about priests from that tribe.
v. 15: the priest who “arises” is like Melchizedek.
v. 16: the basis of his priesthood: not physical descent, but the power of an indestructible life.
v. 17: the proof: Psalm 110:4.
kw: The verb is used of the rising of the sun or a star, and of a shoot springing up. The Greek Old Testament uses the related noun anatolē for the promised “Branch” (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8), and the same noun is what Matthew uses for the star “at its rising” (Matthew 2:2). The Malankara reader hears today's Gospel and epistle speaking the same language.
Literally “a law of a fleshly commandment”. The old priesthood passed from father to son, from one mortal man to the next, because the priests died (7:23).
A word found only here in the New Testament. It means what cannot be loosed or undone. The child born at Yaldo will die, but death will not undo his life, and his priesthood rests on that life.
vv: For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.
This is one of the New Testament's clearest witnesses that Jesus was known to be of the tribe of Judah. See the genealogy in Matthew 1:2–3, and Micah's Bethlehem in today's first reading.
one who has become a priest, not through a legal requirement concerning physical descent, but through the power of an indestructible life.

Christ's priesthood stands on his own risen life. That is why it does not end or pass on to a successor (7:24). Those whom the Church ordains do not replace him; they share in his one priesthood (CCC 1545).
For it is attested of him, “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Jesus himself applies Psalm 110 to the Messiah (Mark 12:35–37), and it is the Old Testament text most quoted in the New Testament. “Forever” is the word that matters here: his priesthood is still at work today.
ch: The Catechism says that the Tradition of the Church considers Melchizedek a prefiguration of the priesthood of Christ, the unique high priest after the order of Melchizedek (CCC 1544), and sees in his offering of bread and wine a foreshadowing of the Church's own offering (CCC 1333). So the Church connects Bethlehem, the house of bread, with the altar: the Child who is born today is the priest and the offering.

From the moment he entered the world, Hebrews says, the Son came to offer himself: “a body you have prepared for me” (10:5). The Second Vatican Council teaches that Christ is present in the Eucharistic sacrifice, in the person of the priest and especially under the Eucharistic species (Sacrosanctum Concilium 7). What the Letter says about his priesthood “forever” is not just a thing of the past.

r.h: The Magi kneel before the Child
set: Herod the Great ruled Judea under Rome from about 37 BC until his death in 4 BC. He was an able builder, who rebuilt the Temple on a grand scale, and a suspicious ruler, who had members of his own family killed. Because he died in 4 BC, Jesus was born a few years before the date our calendar gives, an old miscalculation.

Matthew has already given the genealogy and told of Joseph's dream (ch. 1). He does not describe the birth itself; he goes straight from “he named him Jesus” (1:25) to the arrival of foreigners. His first readers were probably Jewish Christians, and here at the start he shows what the end of his Gospel will command: “make disciples of all nations” (28:19). This is why the Malankara lectionary's Gospel for the feast fits so well: at Yaldo the Church sees not only who was born, but for whom.
str: vv. 1–2: the wise men arrive in Jerusalem with their question.
vv. 3–6: Herod is frightened; the chief priests and scribes find the place in Scripture.
vv. 7–8: Herod's secret meeting and his false request.
vv. 9–10: the star goes before them, and they are overwhelmed with joy.
v. 11: the house, the child with Mary, the homage, and the gifts.
v. 12: the dream and the other road.
¶ The word for homage (proskynein) comes three times: the Magi's aim (v. 2), Herod's lie (v. 8) and the deed itself (v. 11). The whole passage turns on who truly bows down to this child.
kw: Originally a Persian priestly class, and later a general word for men learned in dreams and the stars. Matthew does not call them kings, and he does not say how many there were. Their number three was deduced from the three gifts, while some Syriac writings speak of twelve. “Kings” comes from reading Psalm 72:10 and Isaiah 60:3 alongside this story.
at its rising / in the East
The phrase can mean either. The NRSV reads “at its rising”, the POC “in the East” (കിഴക്ക്). Either way the star recalls Balaam's oracle: “a star shall come out of Jacob” (Numbers 24:17).

To bow to the ground. It can mean homage to a king or worship of God. The POC translates ആരാധിക്കുക, “worship”. Matthew's readers know that the word goes further at the end of his Gospel, when the disciples worship the Risen One (28:17).
The Magi say it first. In Matthew the title returns only in the Passion, in the mouths of Pilate and the soldiers and over the cross (27:11, 29, 37). Between the crib and the cross, the same title.
vv: asking, “Where is the child who has been born king of the Jews? For we observed his star at its rising, and have come to pay him homage.”

They read the sky, and it brings them as far as Jerusalem, but to find the place they need the Scriptures (vv. 4–6). The Catechism draws the lesson: the Magi seek in Israel the Messiah of the nations, and the nations can find him only by turning to the Jews and receiving from them the promises in the Old Testament (CCC 528).
When King Herod heard this, he was frightened, and all Jerusalem with him;

The fear belongs to Herod and those around him; a tyrant's anger put a whole city on edge. This verse says nothing against the Jewish people. Joseph, Mary and Jesus himself are Jews, and it was the Scriptures of Israel that led the way (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The warning is for anyone who knows the Scriptures well but stays at home.
When they saw that the star had stopped, they were overwhelmed with joy.
The Greek piles up the words: they rejoiced with a very great joy. It is the first joy in Matthew's Gospel, and it is felt by foreigners.
On entering the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother; and they knelt down and paid him homage. Then, opening their treasure chests, they offered him gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

“The child with Mary his mother”: Matthew uses this pairing five times in the chapter. The Magi find the Child with his mother, and they kneel to him. The gifts recall Isaiah 60:6 (“gold and frankincense”). St Irenaeus gives the classic reading: gold for a king, incense for God, myrrh for one who would die and be buried (in substance, Against Heresies 3.9.2). Myrrh returns in Nicodemus's burial spices (John 19:39).
And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they left for their own country by another road.
Matthew ends simply, with no further word of them. The old road ran through Herod's palace. Whoever has knelt before Christ does not go home by the same way.
ch: The Catechism sees the Magi, representatives of the neighbouring pagan religions, as the first fruits of the nations, who welcome the good news of salvation through the Incarnation (CCC 528). St Leo the Great, preaching on the Epiphany, calls on all the nations to enter the family of the patriarchs and to adore the Maker of the universe, and sees in the Magi the beginning of what continues in the Church (in substance, Sermons on the Epiphany).

Syriac Christians have long felt close to this story, because the Magi come from the East, the direction of Mesopotamia and Persia, where Syriac Christianity spread. Syriac writings such as the Cave of Treasures tell legends about them. The Church does not read these legends as history, but they show how much the story was loved.

qa: Was Jesus really born on 25 December?

The Gospels do not give the date. The Church's feast is not a birth certificate. It is a day set apart to celebrate a real event. The observance on 25 December is attested at Rome in the fourth century, while many Eastern Churches first kept the Nativity on 6 January. St John Chrysostom, preaching at Antioch around 386, says that the 25 December celebration had been known there for fewer than ten years. The Armenian Apostolic Church still keeps 6 January. What the Church asks us to believe is that the Son of God truly was born of Mary at Bethlehem, in the days of Herod.
Were the Magi three kings? What was the star?

Matthew says neither three nor kings: both are later, reverent readings (see the key word above). As for the star, people have proposed a planetary conjunction, a comet and a new star, and none can be proved. Matthew describes a star that goes before them and stops over a place, and his interest is less in astronomy than in what the star means: God can use even the sky to bring seekers to Christ, and the Scriptures complete the journey.
Why does Matthew's birth story have a house, while Luke has a manger?

Matthew and Luke each tell the story from a different angle, and neither tries to give every detail. Luke describes the night of the birth, with shepherds and a manger. Matthew describes a later visit: the Magi find a “house”, and Herod later orders the killing of children up to two years old (2:16). Yaldo brings the two scenes together, since both are true of the same Child.
rite: In the Malankara tradition the night service of Yaldo includes a fire, lit with frankincense and often with the palm leaves kept from Hosanna Sunday, while the Gloria of the angels is sung. Christ, the Light of the world, is proclaimed as born in the night, as Isaiah says: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (9:2). Today the Yaldo–Denho season begins. It is a joy of this Antiochene family that the Gospel of the feast is the Magi, for they come from the East with their gifts, and Indian Christians who trace their faith to St Thomas may hear this story with special gratitude. At the Holy Qurbono we kneel like the Magi, as if in the village whose name means house of bread, and receive the One who was born there.
study: God chose small Bethlehem. Where in my family or parish is God at work in what seems small, and do I notice it?
The scholars in Jerusalem could name the place, and Matthew does not say that they went. What do I know well about faith but have not yet acted on?
“By another road.” After meeting Christ this Yaldo, what road in my life should I stop taking?
Gold, frankincense, myrrh. What is the most precious thing I could lay before the Child this year?

lead: The day after Yaldo, the Syriac tradition turns in gratitude to the one through whom the Word took flesh. The two readings are very short, and they speak of Mary with very few words. Paul does not even give her name: God sent his Son, “born of a woman”. Luke shows her in silence, while shepherds talk and everyone is amazed: “But Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart”.

Together the readings teach why the Church praises Mary, and how she should be praised. Galatians tells us what happened through her: the eternal Son entered our history and made us children of God. Luke tells us how she lived it: she kept and pondered it. We praise her, and we learn from her. The key words of this day are born, children and treasured.

r.h: Born of a woman
set: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, whom outside teachers are urging to take on circumcision and the Law of Moses. In the verses just before this reading he has compared people under the Law to an heir who is still a child, no better off than a slave until the date set by his father (4:1–3). This is the turning point of the comparison: the date has come.

Galatians is one of the earliest writings of the New Testament, written some decades before the Gospels. These four verses are the only place where Paul refers, even indirectly, to the mother of Jesus. They contain, in a small space, the Father who sends, the Son who is sent, and the Spirit who cries out in our hearts.
str: v. 4: the Father sends his Son, born of a woman, born under the law.
v. 5: the two purposes: to redeem, and to make us children by adoption.
v. 6: the Father sends the Spirit of his Son into our hearts.
v. 7: the conclusion: no longer a slave, but a child and an heir.

¶ The same Greek verb (exapesteilen, “sent”) appears in v. 4 and v. 6. God sends his Son into the world, then sends the Spirit of his Son into our hearts. The first sending happens in the womb of Mary, the second in Baptism.
kw: The time God had set, as a vessel is filled to the brim. It does not mean that the world had become good enough. It means that God's own plan had reached its hour (compare 4:2, “the date set by the father”).

A plain phrase for a truly human birth (compare Job 14:1; Matthew 11:11). Paul is not writing a Marian treatise. He is saying that the Son has a human mother, and so he is one of us. It is exactly this plain phrase that the Council puts at the start of its teaching on Mary (Lumen Gentium 52).
A term from Greek and Roman law. A legally adopted son had full rights in the family and to its inheritance. Jesus is Son by nature; we are made children by grace.

An Aramaic family word for “father”. It was used by Jesus himself in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36) and was kept untranslated in Greek-speaking churches (compare Romans 8:15). It does not simply mean “daddy”, since grown children also used it, but it does carry the warmth of a family.
vv: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,

“Sent” implies that the Son existed before he was born. “Born of a woman” implies that he is truly human. In one verse Paul has the whole faith of Yaldo: truly God's Son, and truly Mary's. “Born under the law” means that he is a son of Israel, circumcised on the eighth day, keeping the Law and fulfilling it.
in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children.

Exagorazō means to buy back, to pay the price of someone's release. It is used for a slave bought out of slavery. The purpose of the Incarnation is told here in a sentence: the Son of God became a son of Mary so that the sons and daughters of Adam might become children of God.
And because you are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”

Paul moves from “you” to “our”, including himself and his readers together. It is the Spirit who cries; Romans 8:15 says that we cry. Christian prayer is the Spirit praying the Son's own prayer in us. The Catechism quotes this verse on the Spirit's work (CCC 742).
So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if a child then also an heir, through God.
“You” is now singular: Paul is speaking to each reader personally. The inheritance is “through God”: it remains a gift to the end.
ch: The Second Vatican Council begins its chapter on Mary in Lumen Gentium with this very text (LG 52). The Catechism cites it in presenting the mystery of Christ (CCC 422), sees in the Annunciation the beginning of “the fullness of time” (CCC 484), and adds that God sent his Son, but asked for the willing co-operation of a creature in preparing a body for him (CCC 488).

St Irenaeus uses the phrase “born of a woman” against those who thought that the Son was not truly human; he says that the Son of God truly took flesh from the Virgin (in substance, Against Heresies 3.22). The Syriac tradition, using its own word Yoldath Aloho, “she who gave birth to God”, holds to the same truth that this verse teaches: the One born of her is God's own Son.

r.h: Mary treasured all these words
set: The angels have just told the shepherds the news: “to you is born this day in the city of David a Savior” (2:11). Bethlehem, David's town, was shepherds' country, the fields where David had kept his father's sheep (1 Samuel 16:11). These people are ordinary working men at the bottom of the social ladder, and God's first announcement of the birth goes to them, and not to the palace.

Luke is the Gospel that shows Mary most closely. Near the start of his Gospel he says that he writes after “investigating everything carefully” (1:3). Twice in the infancy story he describes Mary keeping these things in her heart: here and after the finding in the Temple (2:51). Readers have long wondered whether this is a hint of where some of his information came from. It cannot be proved, but it is a natural thought.
str: v. 15: the shepherds decide to go and see.
v. 16: they go in haste and find Mary, Joseph and the child.
v. 17: they make known what they had been told.
v. 18: all who heard are amazed.
v. 19: Mary treasures and ponders.

¶ The next verse, just past the reading, brings the shepherds back to their sheep, “glorifying and praising God” (2:20). There are three responses in a few lines: the shepherds go and tell, the people wonder, and Mary keeps and ponders.
kw: Here is a detail that the translations hide. The shepherds want to see “this thing that has taken place” (v. 15), and Mary treasures “all these words” (v. 19). It is the same Greek word, rhēma, reflecting the Hebrew dābār, which means both word and event. God's word happens, and what happens speaks.
The Greek of v. 16 has “they went with haste”, and Luke used a closely related phrase for Mary on her way to Elizabeth (1:39). People who have received God's news do not stroll.
To preserve something carefully, keep it whole. The tense suggests a continued action: she went on keeping it.

Literally “to throw together”, to put one thing beside another in order to see how they fit: the angel's words at Nazareth, the census, the manger, the shepherds' story. Mary does not understand everything at once. She gathers it, and she thinks about it in her heart.
vv: When the angels had left them and gone into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, “Let us go now to Bethlehem and see this thing that has taken place, which the Lord has made known to us.”
The shepherds' question is the right one for a believer: God has spoken, so let us go and see. They do not ask for further proof before setting out.
So they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the child lying in the manger.

The sign the angel had given them (2:12) was very ordinary: a baby in a feeding trough. Only faith could see a Savior in it. Mary is named first, then Joseph, and last the child, who is at the centre of the scene.
But Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart.

“But” sets her apart from the amazed crowd. Wonder that does not go deep soon fades. In the Bible the heart is not only the place of feeling, but the centre of a person's thinking and choosing. So Mary is not simply being moved here: she is keeping faith with what she does not yet fully understand.
ch: The Second Vatican Council takes up this verse to describe how the Church's understanding of revelation grows: through the contemplation and study of believers, who treasure these things in their hearts (Dei Verbum 8, citing Luke 2:19, 51; see CCC 94). Mary is therefore not simply a good example. In her, the Church sees what the Church herself is called to do with the Word.

The Council says that the Blessed Virgin advanced in her pilgrimage of faith (Lumen Gentium 58), and St John Paul II writes in Redemptoris Mater that her faith had a real journey. St Augustine says that she conceived Christ in her mind before she conceived him in her womb (in substance, Sermon 215). St Ephrem marvels in his Hymns on the Nativity that Mary is at once her Son's mother, sister and bride (in substance).

qa: Why is there a feast of Mary the day after Christmas? Doesn't it take attention away from Jesus?

It does the reverse. The feast follows Yaldo because it depends on Yaldo: Mary is praised for who was born of her. The Byzantine Churches keep the same day as the Synaxis of the Mother of God, so the custom is broad among Eastern Christians. In this way the Church protects the truth of the Incarnation: he has a real mother, and she is the proof that he is really one of us.
How can a human being be called “Mother of God”? She did not give God his divine nature.

That is correct, and the Church has never said that she did. A mother is mother of a person, not of a nature. The One born of Mary is one Person, the eternal Son of God, who took from her his human nature. So she is truly Mother of God, which is what the Council of Ephesus in 431 confessed in the word Theotokos (CCC 466, 495). The title is first of all a statement about Christ. The Syriac Yoldath Aloho says the same.
Did Mary already know everything about her Son?

The text suggests not. Luke says that she treasured and pondered, and that she and Joseph did not understand what Jesus said in the Temple (2:50). Mary was without sin, but she was not spared the walk of faith. The Council calls it a “pilgrimage of faith” (Lumen Gentium 58). This should encourage believers who also must keep and wait, without understanding everything.
rite: On this second day of Yaldo the Malankara Church praises the Mother of God, as the Syriac Churches have long done. Hymns on Mary fill the West Syriac tradition, from St Ephrem to Mar Jacob of Serugh, whose homilies on the Mother of God are still read, and the faithful honour her in the Holy Qurbono, where the Body born of her is given to us. It is good to keep Christmas in the way this day teaches: to go on holding the mystery in the heart after the crowds and the excitement have gone, as she did.
study: Paul says, “you are no longer a slave but a child”. Where do I still live with God as a slave rather than as a child?
Mary kept and pondered. What word or event from this year do I need to “throw together” with the Word of God, instead of forgetting it?
Shepherds went, told and glorified God. Mary kept it in her heart. Which of these two is harder for me, and which do I need more this Christmas?
How would my family keep Yaldo differently if we kept pondering it after 25 December?

lead: Two days after Yaldo the Church looks at what happened after the shepherds went home: a child growing up in a family. The evening Gospel brings the Holy Family back from Egypt to Nazareth (Matthew 2:19–23). The Old Testament lessons are about children and growth: Isaac, weaned and celebrated, while Hagar and Ishmael are sent away with bread and water and a promise from God (Genesis 21:8–14); the boy Samson, who “grew, and the Lord blessed him” (Judges 13:24–14:4); and Zechariah's picture of a restored Jerusalem, with old people sitting in the streets and “boys and girls playing” (Zechariah 8:3–12). The Catholic Epistle asks the young to accept the authority of the elders and all to “clothe yourselves with humility” (1 Peter 5:5).

The three readings studied here share one word: house. Psalm 122 is the song of pilgrims going up to the house of the Lord. Hebrews says that Christ is faithful over God's house as a son, and that “we are his house”. In Luke the twelve-year-old Jesus is found in the Temple and speaks of his Father for the first time, and then goes down to the small house at Nazareth and obeys. The key words of this Sunday are house, son and growing.

r.h: Let us go to the house of the Lord
set: Of the Old Testament lessons, this psalm stands closest to the Gospel, because it is the song of the very journey Luke describes. Psalms 120–134 each carry the heading “A Song of Ascents”. Most scholars take them as songs linked with going up to Jerusalem for the great feasts. The Law asked Israelite men to appear before the Lord three times a year, at Passover, Weeks and Booths (Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16), and those who could made the journey with family and neighbours.

The heading of this psalm also says “Of David”. David made Jerusalem his capital and brought the ark there (2 Samuel 6), but the Temple was built only by his son. The psalm speaks of the house of the Lord as already standing, so many scholars date it later and read the heading as a dedication to David. In the Greek and Latin Bibles this psalm is numbered 121.
str: vv. 1–2: the joy of the invitation, and the pilgrims' arrival: their feet are standing within the gates.
vv. 3–5: the city itself: built firmly together, the place where the tribes go up to give thanks, the seat of David's house.
vv. 6–9: the prayer for the peace of Jerusalem, “for the sake of my relatives and friends” and “for the sake of the house of the Lord”.
kw: From a verb meaning to go up. Jerusalem stands high in the hills, and one always “goes up” to it, from any direction. The same language appears in Luke: “they went up as usual for the festival” (2:42).

The psalm opens and closes with this phrase (vv. 1, 9). The city matters because the house of God is in it. The joy of the pilgrim is not first in the walls, but in the One who has chosen to be met there.

Peace in the Bible is wholeness and well-being, not only the end of war. In Hebrew verse 6 is a play of sounds, sha’ălû shelôm yerûshālāyim, since people heard the word for peace in the name of Jerusalem. The word comes three times in vv. 6–8.
vv: I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the Lord!”
Going to worship is not a private plan. Someone says “let us go”, and the psalmist is glad to be asked. A family or a parish does this for its members.
Our feet are standing within your gates, O Jerusalem.
After the long road, the pilgrim simply stands and takes it in. The tired feet are part of the prayer.
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem:
The pilgrim is told to pray for the place, and not only to receive from it. Jews, Christians and Muslims all hold Jerusalem dear, and the verse still has its plain meaning today.
For the sake of the house of the Lord our God, I will seek your good.
Love of God's house turns into care for the people around it. Worship that ends in seeking the good of others is what the prophets asked for.
ch: The Catechism says that the Psalms, “prayed and fulfilled in Christ”, are an essential and permanent element of the Church's prayer (CCC 2586). It also says that our visible churches are images of the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem, toward which we are on pilgrimage (CCC 1198). The New Testament speaks of “the Jerusalem above” (Galatians 4:26) and “the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). St Augustine, preaching on this psalm, tells his people that they climb to that city by love, while their feet are still on earth (in substance, Expositions on the Psalms, his Psalm 121).

r.h: Faithful over God's house as a son
set: Hebrews calls itself “a word of exhortation” (13:22). It is a sermon to Christians who were growing tired, some of whom were perhaps tempted to drift away. Chapter 2 has just called Jesus “a merciful and faithful high priest” (2:17). Now the preacher takes up the word “faithful” and compares Jesus with Moses, the greatest figure in Israel's memory.

The comparison rests on one verse. In Numbers 12:7, when Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses, God says of him, “He is entrusted with all my house.” The Greek Old Testament uses the word “faithful” here. Hebrews does not run Moses down. It honours him with the Bible's own words, and then shows a greater honour still.
str: vv. 1–2: “consider that Jesus”, apostle and high priest, faithful as Moses was faithful.
vv. 3–4: the builder has more honour than the house, and the builder of all things is God.
vv. 5–6a: Moses a servant in the house, Christ a son over the house.
v. 6b: the application: we are that house, if we hold firm.
kw: This is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus himself is called an apostle, one who is sent. As apostle he comes from God to us; as high priest he goes on our behalf to God. Moses and Aaron held these two roles between them, and Jesus holds both.
Not the ordinary word for a slave, but a word of honour for one who serves with trust. It comes from Numbers 12:7 in the Greek Old Testament, and appears only here in the New Testament.
The word means both a building and a household, a family. The whole passage plays on this. God's house is not first made of stones but of people.
Literally the boldness to speak openly, the right of a citizen to speak in the assembly. In Hebrews it is the confidence with which we approach God (4:16; 10:19).
vv: consider that Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession,
“Consider” here means to fix the mind on something and study it closely. The cure this preacher offers for tired faith is not a new programme, but a long look at Jesus.
Yet Jesus is worthy of more glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself.
Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that would be spoken later.
Moses' faithfulness is real and it points forward. The Law and the promises were preparing what was to be spoken in the Son (1:1–2).
Christ, however, was faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house if we hold firm the confidence and the pride that belong to hope.

A note on the text: many manuscripts add “firm to the end” after “hope”, and the Malayalam POC has “to the end”. Some of the oldest, including Codex Vaticanus, do not have it here, and the NRSV follows them; the same words stand in v. 14. The meaning does not change. On this Sunday the verse joins Nazareth to us: the Son who obeyed in Joseph's house now has a house of his own, and we are it.
ch: The Catechism names Christ as the “high priest and unique mediator” who has made of the Church a kingdom of priests (CCC 1546), and lists “the house of God in which his family dwells” among the names of the Church (CCC 756). It also takes up the word parrēsia for the simple, trusting boldness with which the Church dares to call God “Father” (CCC 2778). In the Holy Qurbono, Christ the priest stands in the midst of his household, and those who gather around him are the house.

r.h: The boy Jesus in the Temple
set: Luke gives us the only story in the four Gospels from the years between the infancy of Jesus and his baptism. It closes his two chapters on the birth of John and Jesus. These chapters begin in the Temple with Zechariah and end there too. Simeon has just told Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul (2:35); here she has a first taste of that pain.

Passover was one of the three pilgrim feasts, and with the feast of Unleavened Bread it lasted about a week. Nazareth is several days' walk from Jerusalem. People travelled in groups for safety and company, which explains how a boy could be missing for a whole day without alarm. Later Jewish custom held a boy to be bound by the commandments at about thirteen. Age twelve fits a boy coming close to that step, although the bar mitzvah ceremony as we know it is much later.
str: vv. 41–42: the family goes up as usual.
vv. 43–45: Jesus stays; his parents travel a day, search, and return.
vv. 46–47: after three days they find him among the teachers.
v. 48: Mary's question: “Child, why have you treated us like this?”
vv. 49–50: Jesus' first recorded words, which they do not understand.
vv. 51–52: he goes down, obeys and grows; Mary keeps it all.
¶ The words of Jesus stand at the centre, and on both sides of them are the ordinary things: journey, search, return, obedience. Luke places the mystery in the middle of family life.
kw: A company travelling together, used only here in the New Testament. Relatives and neighbours from one village would walk as one body.

A strong word for pain and distress. Luke uses it again for the rich man's agony (16:24–25) and for the grief of the Ephesian elders at parting from Paul (Acts 20:38). Mary's words are not a mild complaint.

The Greek is literally “in the things of my Father”. It can mean “in my Father's house”, as the NRSV has it, or “about my Father's affairs”, as the Malayalam POC has it. Both are sound, since the place and the purpose go together. The small word “must” (dei) is the same one Jesus uses later of his Passion (9:22; 24:26).
The form describes a continuing state: he went on being subject to them. The word used for the years at Nazareth is the plain word for accepting authority.
vv: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
Luke does not show a child lecturing his elders. He listens and asks, and the teachers are the ones amazed (v. 47). Here is a Jewish boy in the house of God among the teachers of his people, at home.
Child, why have you treated us like this? Look, your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety.
Mary calls Joseph “your father”, for so he was in law and in love. The next verse sets another Father beside this one.
Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?
Jesus' first recorded words in Luke speak of his Father, and his last words on the Cross do the same (23:46). The question is not a rebuke. It tells who he is.
But they did not understand what he said to them.
Mary is full of grace, yet she has to walk by faith. Luke is honest about this, and it comforts every parent who has not understood a child, and every believer who has not understood God.
Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart.

The one who has just spoken of his Father goes home and obeys a carpenter and a village mother. This is the longest part of his life on earth, and the Gospels tell almost nothing of it. Luke notes twice that Mary kept these things (2:19, 51). She is the first to keep and ponder the mystery of her Son.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and in years, and in divine and human favor.
Compare the boy Samuel, who “continued to grow both in stature and in favor with the Lord and with the people” (1 Samuel 2:26), and the boy Samson in today's lesson.
ch: The Catechism takes this story as the revelation of Jesus' total consecration to the mission that flows from his divine sonship; Mary and Joseph do not understand, but accept in faith, and Mary keeps all these things in her heart through the years of his hidden life (CCC 534). It calls Nazareth a school, in the words of St Paul VI (CCC 533), and sees in the daily obedience of Jesus to his parents the restoration of what Adam's disobedience destroyed (CCC 532). The Second Vatican Council includes this episode in its teaching on Mary (Lumen Gentium 57), and St John Paul II speaks of Mary's pilgrimage of faith in those hidden years (Redemptoris Mater 17). St Ambrose sees in the three days a sign of the three days before the Resurrection (in substance, Exposition of the Gospel of Luke).

qa: If Jesus is God, how could he grow in wisdom?

The Son of God took a true human soul, and with it true human knowledge, which by its nature develops in time and experience. So he could truly “increase in wisdom” (CCC 472). The Church also teaches that this human knowledge, through its union with the divine Word, expressed the divine life of his person, and that he knew what he had come to reveal (CCC 473–474). One person, true God and true man: he does not pretend to grow.
Was Jesus disobedient or unkind to his parents?

Luke does not present it so. In the next breath he says that Jesus “was obedient to them”. He does not excuse Mary's pain or blame her for asking. The story shows that his Father's claim comes first, and that this first claim is what makes him a true son at home. Every family that gives a child to God's service knows something of this.
Today's lectionary lists Hebrews as an Epistle of St Paul. Did Paul write it?

The letter does not name its author, and its Greek style differs from Paul's. Many in the early Eastern Churches held it to be Paul's, or to come from his circle. Origen, as Eusebius reports, said that God alone knows who wrote it down (in substance). The Church has always received it as inspired Scripture and read it with Paul's letters, as the Malankara lectionary does. Its authority does not depend on settling the question.
rite: Yaldo means birth in Syriac, and the Sundays after it stay with the Child. The Syriac tradition is especially fond of wonder at this mystery: St Ephrem, in his Hymns on the Nativity, has Mary marvel at the Child she carries and adores (in substance). For the Malankara family this Sunday has a plain message. The road from Nazareth to Jerusalem and back is the road from home to church and back. When a family comes together to the Holy Qurbono and goes home to obey, serve and pray, it walks the way the Holy Family walked, and the Catechism calls such a home a domestic Church (CCC 1655–1657, 2204). Mary's way of keeping things in her heart is also a good rule for mothers, fathers and grandparents who hand on the faith through many small, unrecorded years.
study: Psalm 122 begins with someone saying “let us go”. Who first brought me to the house of the Lord? For whom could I be that voice?
Hebrews 3:6 says “we are his house”. What would change in my parish if we took this seriously?
Mary and Joseph “did not understand”, yet they kept faith. What in my life or my family do I not yet understand, and how can I keep it before God as Mary did?
Jesus spent most of his life in the hidden obedience of Nazareth. What ordinary duty of this week can I offer as he did?

lead: The day's title names David, King and Prophet, and both readings speak of him. Hebrews places David in the long line of those who lived by faith and did not yet receive what was promised. In Matthew, Jesus asks how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord. Three days after Yaldo, the question points straight to the Child of Bethlehem, born in David's town.

r.h: Through faith they conquered kingdoms
set: Hebrews 11 is the great roll of faith, from Abel onward. The preacher has reached the judges and kings, and sees that he cannot go through them one by one: “time would fail me”. So he lists a few names and then a string of deeds, and those who know the Scriptures can fill in the stories. The chapter prepares for the climax in 12:1–2, where these witnesses surround us and Jesus is “the pioneer and perfecter of our faith”.
str: v. 32: the names: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, the prophets.
vv. 33–35a: faith that won visible victories.
vv. 35b–38: faith that seemed to lose: torture, chains, death, homelessness.
vv. 39–40: none of them received the promise yet; God kept something better.
kw: Literally “having been witnessed to”. God himself bears witness to them. The same family of words gives us “martyr” and “witnesses” in 12:1.
One of the favourite words of Hebrews: a better hope, a better covenant, better promises (7:19, 22; 8:6). What is better is what God has given in Christ.
To be brought to the goal. The saints of Israel reach it together with us, through Christ, and not apart from us.
vv: And what more should I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets
The list includes people with grave faults, and Scripture does not hide David's sin (2 Samuel 11–12). The faith that the list honours is trust in God, kept or found again.
who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions,

David fits every phrase: he subdued kingdoms (2 Samuel 8), he did justice for his people (2 Samuel 8:15), and he received the promise of a lasting house (2 Samuel 7). The lions recall Daniel in the den (Daniel 6:22), and also David and Samson.
Others were tortured, refusing to accept release, in order to obtain a better resurrection.

Probably the martyrs of the Maccabean persecution, Eleazar and the seven brothers (2 Maccabees 6–7). “Sawn in two” in v. 37 recalls a Jewish tradition about the death of Isaiah. A note on the text: in v. 37 some manuscripts have another word in the list, “they were tested”, which the POC includes in its own wording and the NRSV omits.
Yet all these, though they were commended for their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better so that they would not, apart from us, be made perfect.
The Church before Christ and the Church after him are one people of faith, moving toward one goal.
ch: The Catechism says that the Old Testament is rich in witnesses to faith, and that the “something better” God foresaw is the grace of believing in his Son (CCC 147). It tells us to look to this cloud of witnesses (CCC 165), and it calls David the king “after God's own heart”, the shepherd who prays for his people and in their name (CCC 2579).

r.h: David's son and David's Lord
set: We are in Jerusalem, in the last days before the Passion. Jesus has been questioned in the Temple about the tax to Caesar, the resurrection and the greatest commandment (22:15–40). Now he asks the question himself. Many in Israel hoped for a king from David's line, on the strength of God's promise in 2 Samuel 7:12–16 and of texts like Isaiah 11:1, and the Pharisees give the expected answer. Jesus does not deny it. He shows that it is not the whole answer.
str: vv. 41–42: Jesus' question, and the answer: “The son of David.”
vv. 43–45: Psalm 110:1, and the riddle it raises.
v. 46: silence, and the end of the questions.
kw: the Lord said to my Lord

In Hebrew the two words differ: the first is the Name of God, the second means “my lord”, a title for a king or master. The Greek Bible has kyrios for both, and so the Christian ear hears the Father speaking to the Son.
Jesus treats the psalm as a word given by the Holy Spirit. Acts calls David a prophet for the same reason (Acts 2:30), which fits today's title.
The anointed one. Kings of Israel were anointed; David was anointed by Samuel at Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:13).
vv: What do you think of the Messiah? Whose son is he?
This is the question of the whole Gospel, and it stands in front of each reader.
The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet”
Psalm 110 is the Old Testament text most often quoted or echoed in the New. In a culture where a father does not call his son “lord”, the question has real force.
If David thus calls him Lord, how can he be his son?

The answer is not given in words. The reader of Matthew already knows it: he is “the son of David” (1:1) and also “God is with us” (1:23). He is David's son by birth and David's Lord as Son of God. Compare Romans 1:3–4.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus ascribes the title “Lord” to himself in a veiled way when he disputes with the Pharisees about the meaning of Psalm 110 (CCC 447). It also teaches that Christ's sitting at the right hand of the Father is the start of the Messiah's kingdom (CCC 663–664). The Fathers, and the Council of Chalcedon after them, taught the mystery this text points to: one person, true God and true man.

qa: Did David really write Psalm 110?

The heading says “Of David”, and in Jesus' day this was the common understanding. Jesus' argument starts from that shared ground. Many scholars today think of the Psalter as growing over time around David's name. Whatever the history of the text, the Church reads Psalm 110 as inspired and fulfilled in Christ, which is the point Jesus is making.
rite: David's voice is never far away in the Malankara Church, since the Psalms run through its daily prayer and its liturgy. To remember him in this week of Yaldo is to remember the promise that brought the Child to Bethlehem.
study: Hebrews 11 honours people who “did not receive what was promised”. What am I still waiting for from God, and how can I keep faith while I wait?
Jesus asks, “What do you think of the Messiah?” How would I answer him today, in my own words?

lead: Today's two readings ask whether we can trust God's mercy and whether we honour him with the heart. Paul looks at God's plan for Israel and the nations and ends in mercy for all. In Matthew, Jesus takes up a question about washing hands and turns it into a question about caring for one's parents and the state of one's heart. The first reading warns against pride, and the second warns against empty religion.

r.h: The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's long reflection, in sorrow and in hope, on why most of his own people had not accepted Jesus as Messiah. He is a Jew who loves his people (9:1–5). In 11:17–24 he has told Gentile Christians that they are wild olive branches grafted onto Israel's tree, and that they must not boast. Today's passage is the conclusion of the argument. It is also one of the key texts for the Church's teaching about the Jewish people.
str: vv. 25–27: the mystery: a hardening on part of Israel, until the Gentiles have come in, “and so all Israel will be saved”.
vv. 28–29: enemies as regards the gospel, beloved as regards election.
vv. 30–32: disobedience and mercy, for both groups, for all.
kw: In Paul not a riddle but God's plan, once hidden and now made known.
Partial and temporary, in Paul's words. He does not say that God has rejected his people; he has already said the opposite (11:1–2).
Literally “not to be regretted”, things God does not take back. The word is the foundation of what follows.
vv: And so all Israel will be saved; as it is written, “Out of Zion will come the Deliverer; he will banish ungodliness from Jacob.”
The quotation joins Isaiah 59:20–21 and 27:9. Paul does not say when or how, and he does not explain it further. He leaves it in God's hands and ends in praise (11:33–36).
As regards the gospel they are enemies of God for your sake; but as regards election they are beloved, for the sake of their ancestors; for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.

In the Greek, “of God” is added by the translators, and it is not a word for Christians to use as an insult. Paul's point is the second half: they are beloved. The Second Vatican Council quotes these verses in teaching that the Jews remain very dear to God (Nostra Aetate 4; Lumen Gentium 16).
For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.
Everyone stands on the same ground. Nobody earns mercy, and nobody is outside its reach.
ch: The Catechism quotes this chapter when it speaks of the Church's relationship with the Jewish people, “the first to hear the Word of God” (CCC 839). Elsewhere it states that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121). It reads “all Israel” in connection with the coming of Christ in glory (CCC 674). It takes v. 32 as a summary of the mystery of sin and grace (CCC 1870). A Vatican document of 2015 on Catholic-Jewish relations takes its title from v. 29, The Gifts and the Calling of God Are Irrevocable.

r.h: Honouring God with lips, not hearts
set: A group of Pharisees and scribes comes from Jerusalem to Galilee to question Jesus. The Pharisees were a respected lay movement within Judaism, who wanted all Israel to live in holiness in daily life. So they extended to ordinary meals some of the washing the Law asked of priests. This is not a question of hygiene, but of ritual purity. Jesus is disputing here as a Jew among Jews, and strong language was usual in such arguments. Matthew's words are not about the Jewish people as a whole (Nostra Aetate 4).
str: vv. 1–2: the charge: your disciples do not wash before eating.
vv. 3–6: Jesus' counter-charge, with one example: the commandment to honour parents, set aside by a vow.
vv. 7–9: Isaiah's word about lips and hearts.
kw: The body of teaching handed down to explain and apply the Law. Later Judaism wrote much of it down in the Mishnah.

A gift offered to God. The parallel in Mark 7:11 gives the Hebrew word korban. A son could declare his goods dedicated, and then say he had nothing for his parents. The later rabbis themselves discussed ways to release a person from such vows for the sake of parents' honour.
In Greek, a stage actor, one who speaks from behind a mask. The word fits what follows: lips without the heart.
vv: And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?
Jesus does not attack the Law. He defends it, and he defends one of the Ten Commandments in particular.
So, for the sake of your tradition, you make void the word of God.
Any believer, of any time, can do this: use religious duty as an escape from plain love.
This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me;
Isaiah 29:13, in the form close to the Greek Old Testament. Isaiah spoke it as a prophet within Israel to his own people. It is addressed to us each time we pray.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus confronted certain human traditions of the Pharisees that were making God's word void (CCC 581), and it recalls this very passage in teaching the duty of grown children to support their parents in old age (CCC 2218). It also says, “If our heart is far from God, the words of prayer are in vain” (CCC 2562).

qa: Is Jesus rejecting all tradition? Doesn't the Church value Tradition?

Jesus rejects a human custom that cancels God's command. The Church distinguishes the apostolic Tradition, which hands on the faith received from Christ, from the many customs and practices that grow up in the Church and can be changed or dropped if they no longer serve (CCC 83). The test Jesus gives holds for all our customs: do they help us love God and neighbour, or do they give us a way around it?
study: Paul warns against being “wiser than you are”. Where do I look down on others, as if God's mercy were my own achievement?
Is there any religious habit of mine that has become a way of avoiding a duty to a parent, a spouse or a neighbour?

lead: Paul asks a divided community to welcome one another, because Christ came to confirm God's promises to Israel and to bring the nations to praise. He ends with “the root of Jesse” from Isaiah. The Gospel takes the Holy Family back from Egypt to an unknown village, where the promised one will be called a Nazorean. Both readings show God keeping his word in unexpected ways.

r.h: The God of hope
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome in the later 50s, probably from Corinth. He did not found that Church. It seems to have had believers of both Jewish and Gentile background, who differed about food and holy days. Chapters 14 and 15 address this tension, speaking of the “weak” and the “strong”. Today's passage draws it together: both groups are one in Christ, and Scripture has always foreseen it.
str: v. 7: the command: welcome one another, as Christ has welcomed you.
vv. 8–9a: Christ served the circumcised for God's truth, and the Gentiles for God's mercy.
vv. 9b–12: four quotations: Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1, Isaiah 11:10.
v. 13: a closing blessing: the God of hope.
kw: To take someone to oneself, to receive into one's home and circle. The word opened this section (14:1), and God is its subject there too (14:3).
Jesus is a Jew who served his own people, to keep God's word to their ancestors. Paul says this to Gentile Christians, so that they will not forget it.
The shoot from David's family (Isaiah 11:1, 10). Today's Gospel may echo the same chapter.
vv: Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
The welcome is measured by Christ's welcome, not by how much we like one another.
The root of Jesse shall come, the one who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope.
Paul's chain of texts draws on the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms: all of Scripture is singing the same song.
May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
Hope, in Paul, is not an optimistic temperament. It comes from God, and it grows in believing.
ch: The Catechism quotes this blessing as the prayer of hope (CCC 2657) and describes hope as the virtue by which we rely not on our own strength but on the help of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1817). The welcome Paul asks for marks the Church, which is one people gathered from all nations (CCC 831).

r.h: He will be called a Nazorean
set: Herod the Great died about 4 BC, and Augustus divided his kingdom among his sons. Archelaus received Judea. According to Josephus, he began his reign with a harsh crackdown at Passover in which many died, and he was finally deposed and banished in AD 6. Herod Antipas received Galilee. So Joseph's fear was reasonable. Nazareth was a small village, not mentioned in the Old Testament, in a region that Judeans did not much regard (compare John 1:46).
str: vv. 19–20: the dream in Egypt: go back to the land of Israel.
v. 21: Joseph obeys.
v. 22: fear of Archelaus, and a second warning.
v. 23: Nazareth, and the fulfilment.
kw: Matthew hears the place name in this title. Two Old Testament words are often suggested: nēṣer, the “branch” from Jesse (Isaiah 11:1), and nāzîr, one consecrated to God, as Samson was (Judges 13:5). No one is sure which Matthew had in mind, and he may be thinking of both.
Literally “take along with you”. Joseph is told to take “the child and his mother”, the same phrase that recurs through this chapter (2:13, 14, 20, 21).
vv: Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child’s life are dead.
This echoes God's word to Moses: “all those who were seeking your life are dead” (Exodus 4:19). Matthew shows Jesus reliving Israel's story and the story of Moses.
Then Joseph got up, took the child and his mother, and went to the land of Israel.
Joseph says nothing in this Gospel. He is told and he does, in almost the same words.
There he made his home in a town called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, “He will be called a Nazorean.”

No Old Testament verse has these exact words. The Greek says “through the prophets”, in the plural (the POC has the singular), which suggests a general sense of prophecy and not one text. St Jerome draws this very conclusion: Matthew takes the sense of the Scriptures and not their words (in substance).
ch: The Catechism sees in the return from Egypt the Exodus story, with Jesus as the definitive liberator (CCC 530), and it treats the years at Nazareth as Jesus' sharing in the daily life of most people (CCC 531–533). Pope Francis, in Patris Corde 3, draws from Joseph's dreams the portrait of an obedient father, who at each step does as he is told.

study: Who is the person in my parish or family that I find it hardest to “welcome”? What would Christ's welcome look like toward them?
Joseph acted at once on a word he could only half understand. What small step of obedience is before me now?

lead: The year ends with a question about fruit. Paul looks back on years of work, and calls it all a priestly offering and the work of Christ, not his own. In Luke, a gardener begs for one more year for a barren fig tree. Together they teach us to look back with thanks and to look ahead with repentance, since another year is itself a mercy.

r.h: The priestly service of the gospel
set: Paul is coming to the end of his letter. He had not yet visited Rome, and has written boldly to a Church he did not found. He now explains why: his calling is to the Gentiles. He has worked from Jerusalem to Illyricum, the Roman province on the eastern coast of the Adriatic, and now plans to go on to Spain, by way of Rome (15:24). Acts does not tell of any work in Illyricum, so this verse is our only direct word on it.
str: vv. 14–15a: praise for the Romans, and a courteous word about his boldness.
vv. 15b–16: his calling, in the language of worship.
vv. 17–19: what Christ has done through him.
vv. 20–21: his ambition, to preach where Christ is not yet named, with Isaiah 52:15.
kw: A word for public service, and in the Greek Old Testament often for priests and Levites serving in the Temple. English “liturgy” comes from the same family.
Literally “serving as a priest”, used only here in the New Testament. Paul uses the word for preaching the Gospel.
The offering here is the Gentiles themselves, converted and sanctified by the Spirit, placed before God.
vv: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.
Evangelising and worship are not two separate things. The aim of preaching is to bring people to God as an offering.
For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me
Paul has the gift of looking back without boasting of himself. “Through me” is all he claims.
Thus I make it my ambition to proclaim the good news, not where Christ has already been named, so that I do not build on someone else’s foundation,
Paul does not criticise those who build on others' foundations; he speaks of his own call. Yet the question is open to all of us: to whom has Christ not yet been named?
ch: The Catechism points out that in the New Testament the word “liturgy” refers not only to divine worship but also to proclaiming the Gospel and to active charity (CCC 1070), and it cites this verse. The Second Vatican Council uses this verse to describe the work of priests, whose preaching leads to the offering of the faithful, joined to the one sacrifice of Christ (Presbyterorum Ordinis 2).

r.h: Let it alone for one more year
set: Just before this, people tell Jesus of Galileans killed by Pilate, and he himself mentions the people killed when the tower of Siloam fell. He says that these people were not worse sinners than others, and that all must repent (13:1–5). The parable follows at once, and shows why there is still time. The vine and the fig tree are familiar images of God's people in the prophets (Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1), but here the words are addressed to every hearer who has heard the call to repent.
str: v. 6: a fig tree, and no fruit.
v. 7: the owner: three years, “Cut it down!”
vv. 8–9: the gardener's plea, and the open ending.
kw: To make useless. A fig tree takes water and nutrients from the soil, and a barren one takes them from the vines too.
The verb aphiēmi means to leave alone, and it is also the Gospel word for forgiving. Luke's readers would know it from the Lord's Prayer (11:4).
An unattractive detail, and an honest one. Care for a barren tree is patient and dirty work.
vv: See here! For three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and still I find none. Cut it down! Why should it be wasting the soil?
The owner's complaint is not unjust. The parable takes judgment seriously, and it does not make light of a life without fruit.
Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it.
The gardener does not only ask for time. He promises to work. Many readers see Christ in him, the one who intercedes for us and works on us.
If it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.
Luke does not tell us what happened, and the parable stops here. The end of the story is left to the hearer.
ch: St Augustine takes the three years as the three ages of human history, before the Law, under the Law and under grace, and hears in the gardener the voice of those who plead for the Church (in substance, Sermon 110). St Gregory the Great sees in the manure the memory of one's sins, which brings the soul to repentance and fruitfulness (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 31). The Catechism speaks of God's patience, who wants “all to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9; CCC 1037), and calls conversion a turning of the whole life that is the work of God's grace (CCC 1431–1432).

qa: Is God the harsh owner, and Jesus the kind gardener?

No. The parable is not setting the Father against the Son. The Son reveals the Father's own patience (2 Peter 3:9), and it is the Father who sends him. The owner and the gardener together teach two truths: God really looks for fruit, and God really gives us time.
rite: On the last day of the year, this parable makes a good examination of conscience for a Malankara home or parish before the Holy Qurbono of the new year: what fruit has the year borne, what has been wasted, and what must I ask the Lord to dig around and feed in the coming year?
study: Looking back on this year as Paul does, what has Christ accomplished through me, even in small ways? How do I thank him?
If this coming year is my “one more year”, what fruit does the Lord most want to find?
